### MINUTES OF THE FORTY-SEVENTH GENERAL

### ASSEMBLY

First Session – Wednesday Afternoon June 26, 2019

47-1 Assembly Called to Order and Opening Worship The Forty-seventh General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America gathered at 1:30 p.m. on Wednesday, June 26, 2019, at the Hilton Anatole in Dallas, Texas, for the opening worship service and observance of the Lord's Supper. Outgoing Moderator TE Irwyn Ince Jr. called the Assembly to order for worship (see Appendix X, p. 732).

Following worship, the Assembly recessed at 3:00 p.m. to reconvene at 3:30 p.m.

47-2 Assembly Reconvenes – Declaration of Quorum and Enrollment The Moderator reconvened the Assembly at 3:00 p.m. for business. TE Charles Knight led in prayer. The Moderator declared a quorum present, with 407 Ruling Elders and 1160 Teaching Elders (1567 total) enrolled (see Appendix S, p. 519 for complete Attendance Report).

47-3 Election of Moderator  
The Moderator opened the floor for nominations for Moderator of  
the Forty-seventh General Assembly. TE Bryan Chapell placed in nomination  
RE J. Howard “Howie" Donahoe. TE Ronnie Garcia placed in nomination  
RE John R. Bise. The Moderator declared nominations closed, and RE Donahoe  
was elected Moderator (848-493).  
RE Howard Donahoe, Moderator of the 47th PCA General Assembly,  
assumed the chair and addressed the court.  
RE Todd Carlisle, Chairman of the Administrative Committee,  
presented to retiring Moderator Ince a plaque in token of the Assembly's  
appreciation for his year of service as Moderator.

47-13 Interchurch Relations Committee Informational and Committee of Commissioner Reports and Fraternal Greetings (continued from 47-10, p. 19) TE Bruce O'Neil, Chairman of the Permanent Committee on Interchurch Relations introduced Dr. Davi Charles Gomes of the Brazilian Presbyterian Church, who brought fraternal greetings on behalf of his denomination and the World Reformed Fellowship. CoC Chairman Barnes continued with the report of the Committee of Commissioners on Interchurch Relations. TE Barnes presented as a substitute motion the Committee of Commissioner's Recommendation 5, to answer Overture 23 (“Withdraw from the National Association of Evangelicals") in the affirmative. He noted that the grounds for the recommendation (which were included in the distributed copy) should be struck, as they had been included as part of the recommendation in error. <a id="ga47-p23"></a>

TE Bruce O'Neil, Chairman of the Permanent Committee, presented the recommendation of the Permanent Committee (RAO 14-6.h), that Overture 23 be answered in the negative TE Carl Robbins, presented arguments on behalf of the CoC's substitute motion. TE O'Neil then responded on behalf the Permanent Committee. Floor debate ensued. A point of order was raised, citing RAO 19-4.d, that debate was not being limited to three minutes per person. The Moderator ruled that the point of order was not well taken because RAO 14-9.h applies at this point. TE Josh Owen asked for clarification on what the Assembly will be voting on when the debate is closed. The Moderator summarized the question upon which commissioners would be voting. TE Allan Taha moved to call the question. Upon the advice of the parliamentarians that debate shall not be limited, the Moderator ruled that calling the question was not permitted at this point. Debate continued. TE Fred Greco made a parliamentary inquiry regarding the earlier motion to move the previous question. Citing RAO 14-9.e and RONR (11th ed.), p. 65, ll. 14-19, he argued that moving the previous question is not a move to limit debate, but to close debate. The Moderator referred the matter to the parliamentarians and allowed the debate to continue. The time for debate having expired, Permanent Committee Chairman O'Neil yielded his time to TE Roy Taylor, Stated Clerk, who gave the final word (RAO 19-4.b). in favor of the Permanent Committee's recommendation to answer Overture 23 in the negative. The Assembly proceeded to a vote on the CoC's Recommendation 5, to answer Overture 23 in the affirmative. The recommendation failed (590- 845), The Assembly then voted on Recommendation 5 of the Permanent Committee, which was adopted by voice vote, answering Overture 23 in the negative and thereby indicating the Assembly's decision to remain in the National Association of Evangelicals (NAE). TE Per Almquist raised a point of order that the Assembly had not voted on Recommendation 6 of the IRC. The Moderator ruled the point of order well taken, presented IRC Recommendation 6, and seeing no opposition, declared Recommendation 6 adopted by common consent.

### PARTIAL REPORT OF THE OVERTURES COMMITTEE

### TO THE FORTY-SEVENTH GENERAL ASSEMBLY

### OF THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA

IV. Recommendations

6. That Overture 6 from Pacific Northwest Presbytery ("Amend RAO 11 and 13 to Disallow Memorials") be answered in the affirmative. Adopted Grounds: While Memorial overtures have historical precedent in the PCA, recent history suggests that they may be problematic. There is no provision in the RAO to prevent negative content from being included. There is also no good mechanism for determining who should or should not be memorialized by the Assembly.

12. That Overture 12 from Northern New England Presbytery (“Amend RAO 8-4 regarding Floor Nominations") be answered in the negative. Adopted Grounds: The nomination and election processes have served the PCA well for decades. The current process is the balanced influence of Presbyteries, a representative General Assembly committee, and the General Assembly at large.

16. That Overture 16 from Georgia Foothills Presbytery (“Amend the RAO to Provide for a Moderator-Elect and Vice-Moderator by Revision of RAO 1-4, Addition of RAO 1-6, 1-7, and 1-8, and Revision of RAO 2-1, 2-3") be answered in the negative. Adopted Grounds: There has never been a problem with current election procedure. The proposed amendment would not give the Assembly the ability to choose a Moderator based on the issues before that Assembly.

18. That Overture 18 from Houston Metro Presbytery (“Amend RAO 11-5 to Prevent Confusion and Possible Contradictory Actions on Overtures by Multiple Committees of Commissioners") be answered in the affirmative as amended (For OC changes, <del class="double-strikethrough">double strike</del><del class="double-strikethrough">through</del> for deletions, double underlining for additions; single underlining for original additions in overture). Adopted Therefore, be it resolved, that the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America amend RAO 11-5 with the following additions (additions are underlined): 11-5. Upon receipt the Stated Clerk shall refer all overtures requesting amendment of the Book of Church Order or the Rules of Assembly Operations to the Committee on Constitutional Business for its advice to the Overtures Committee. Upon receipt, the Stated Clerk shall forward all overtures concerning presbytery boundaries or a new presbytery to the permanent Committee on Mission to North America. Any overture, other than an overture proposing amendment to the Constitution (which shall be referred to the Committee on Constitutional Business for its advice to the Overtures Committee), having to do with the nature or responsibilities of a permanent Committee or Agency shall be referred by the Clerk to the appropriate permanent Committee or Agency or ad interim committee. All other overtures shall be referred to the Overtures Committee. <del class="double-strikethrough">No overture shall be</del> <del class="double-strikethrough">referred for consideration and recommendation to</del> <del class="double-strikethrough">more than one Committee of Commissioners, permanent</del> 25

<del class="double-strikethrough">Committee or Agency or ad interim committee; an</del> <del class="double-strikethrough">overture, however, may be referred for informational</del> <del class="double-strikethrough">purposes only to another Committee of Commissioners</del>, <del class="double-strikethrough">permanent Committee or Agency or ad interim</del> <del class="double-strikethrough">eommittee</del>. An overture proposing amendment to the Constitution shall be referred only to the Overtures Committee for consideration and recom-mendation; such an overture, however, may be referred to other Committees of Commissioners, other permanent Committees or Agencies, or other ad interim committees for advice only, to the Overtures Committee. All overtures shall be published in the Commissioner Handbook with reference for consideration indicated. Grounds: This Overture is needed to prevent contradictory recommendations on overtures from multiple committees with respect to Constitutional amendments. Respectfully submitted, TE Sean Lucas, Chairman RE Edward L. Wright, Secretary

9. That Overture 24 from Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery “Add Constitutional Precedence Statement to Policy Manuals" be answered with reference to the recommendation from the Administrative Committee regarding Overture 24. Adopted

10. That Overture 41 from Heritage Presbytery, "Direct CMTW to Amend its Guidelines to Implement CMTW’s ‘Statement on Valuing Women in MTW,' so that only Ordained Elders Will Be Allowed to Serve in the Roles of Team Leader, Regional Director, and International Director within MTW," (p.153) be answered in the negative. With the following grounds recorded as part of the motion. Grounds: In formulating and finalizing its “Statement on Valuing Women," CMTW carefully considered the report on the ad interim committee to the 45th General Assembly and believes that its statement on valuing women in MTW is wholly consistent with the ad interim report in all material respects. Mission to World, CMTW, and the General Assembly have approved unordained men to the roles of team leader, country director, and regional director since 1983 and at least 3 women since around 2006. We have identified at least 35 unordained leaders appointed to these positions since 2003. CMTW and GA have never required these positions be held exclusively by ordained elders.

34

<a id="ga47-p37"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=37 printed_page=35 -->

MTW teams vary extensively across the globe. While the ultimate aim of all our teams is to plant and revitalize churches, not all of our teams have ordained elders engaged directly in planting churches. Some teams are focused on facilitative church planting where our missionaries work alongside ordained national partners who are leading churches and church plants. Others are focused on university ministries (Christ's College team in Taiwan), medical ministries, mercy ministries (Ethiopia), education ministries, etc. to make disciples who fill local churches and church plants. In some cases there are a variety of different ministries all under the umbrella of one team. The overture would unnecessarily restrict unordained men and women from serving in roles that do not require ordination. The overture if passed would immediately affect 19 unordained missionaries who are serving in these roles across the globe as well as their teams. These leaders would be removed from their positions, receive less remuneration, and would have to find new roles on the team. It would also require taking 19 ordained missionaries out of their current ministry roles to take their places. CMTW and the coordinator are committed to working with those whose consciences are affected by women or unordained men serving in leadership in non-ecclesial roles over (ordained) men. We want to move forward together in a manner that does not hinder the work of the Kingdom. The principle that unordained leaders defer matters of the church to ordained leaders in line authority has been MTW's practice for many years. Women and unordained men in leadership over TE church planters routinely defer matters related to the church to other ordained supervisors. While this practice necessarily involves linedrawing, in practice this line-drawing has not proved to be an unsurmountable problem, and we pledge to continue to ensure that church matters be referred to the proper ordained authorities. The authority given to team leaders for spiritual care of their members does not necessitate ordination. Spiritual care can be given by unordained believers. Team leaders can also delegate to others to provide spiritual care as is appropriate. Finally, while CMTW has non-voting women advisors, CMTW is not proposing the addition of women to serve on CMTW through this statement. Adopted IV. 12. The Covenant Seminary Board of Trustees voted unanimously at its April 26, 2019, stated meeting to recommend that Overture 2 from Northwest Georgia Presbytery, “Encourage CTS toward Growth and Release from Assembly Oversight," be answered in the negative with the following rationale. Adopted Rationale: Covenant Seminary was shocked to hear of this overture as we were in no way consulted on this overture. Covenant Seminary does not and never has desired to be released from PCA oversight but rather delights in and values deeply the oversight provided through the General Assemblyelected ruling and teaching elders. Contrary to the implication of the overture, Covenant Seminary has every desire to continue to be under the exclusive oversight of ordained elders as voting members of the Board of Trustees. Covenant Seminary believes that authoritative oversight of the Seminary by ordained elders is particularly important and vital for the task of training men who will be ordained pastors in the PCA. Then Covenant Seminary President Dr. Will Barker stated at the 10th General Assembly that "theological education should be under the denomination's—auspices and responsible to the church. Our history has been blessed through this orientation to the work of the church." We continue to believe this, desire this, and are blessed by this official and formal relationship. Between 1981 and 1982 all 25 PCA presbyteries voted to receive the RPCES into the PCA with the understanding that Covenant College and Covenant Seminary would be received into the PCA and have their own Committees of Commissioners at General Assembly. Elders who serve on the Board of Trustees are recommended by presbyteries to the GA Nominating Committee, which then recommends an annual slate of board nominees who are voted on by the General Assembly. The members of the Board of Trustees elect the president, approve faculty members, adopt the budget, and oversee the Seminary's doctrinal and educational work of training, equipping, and sending graduates into the church.

40

<a id="ga47-p43"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=43 printed_page=41 -->

Elected members of the Board of Trustees annually reaffirm by signature their commitment to the system of doctrine taught in the Westminster Standards. The approval of the General Assembly Theological Examining Committee is necessary for each newly elected president to take up the office of president. The Presbytery-elected Committee of Commissioners reviews the work of the Seminary each year and brings recommendations to the General Assembly. The above-named oversight and accountability provide mutual benefit to the PCA and to Covenant Seminary by maintaining our shared conviction to be faithfully committed to the inerrancy of the Bible, the historic Reformed faith, and the great commission. It is our deep desire and delight to continue to serve as the denominational seminary of the PCA as we strive to "glorify the triune God by training his servants to walk in God's grace, minister God's Word, and equip God's people—all for God's mission."

9. That Overture 11 from Fellowship Presbytery "Commend and Distribute RPCNA's ‘Contemporary Perspectives on Sexual Orientation: A Theological and Pastoral Analysis" be answered in the negative. Adopted Grounds:

- **(1)** The report mentioned in the Overture was published by Crown & Covenant Publications in 2012 under the title The Gospel & Sexual Orientation (Michael Lefebvre, Editor). Given that the material is under copyright with Crown & Covenant Publications and The Synod of the Reformed Presbyterian Church of North America (RPCNA), the overture is improper and out of order in that it asks the GA and CDM to do something that would require legal permission which they do not currently have (RRO 39, 11th ed., p. 343).

- **(2)** The Gospel & Sexual Orientation is in print and available from CDM through the PCA Bookstore (pcabookstore.com, item #11555). It is also available publicly at the URL indicated in the Overture.

- **(3)** The overture directs the production of curriculum without any consideration for the proper funding to complete the project (see also point 1 above).

10. That Overture 24 from Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery “Add Constitutional Precedence Statement to Policy Manuals" be answered by reference to the recommendation from the Administrative Committee regarding Overture 24 (see p. 66). Adopted

11. That Overture 25 from Suncoast Florida Presbytery "Support Christian Education" be answered in the negative. Adopted Grounds:

- **(1)** The overture is unnecessary. Scripture clearly teaches that parents have the responsibility for the education of covenant children (Deut. 6, Eph. 6). Church Sessions have the power "to determine the best measures for promoting the spiritual interests of the church and congregation”(BCO 12-5.e). The General Assembly does not need to affirm what Scripture clearly teaches and the Constitution already provides.

- **(2)** The particular method(s) used by parents to fulfill their scriptural responsibility is a matter of conscience, guided by the Holy Spirit and informed by the Word of God and the pastoral counsel of elders in the local church. It is inappropriate for the General Assembly to direct parents (explicitly or implicitly) to a particular method. The overture may (unintentionally) bind the conscience of a parent attempting to fulfill his/her scriptural responsibility. 59

<a id="ga47-p62"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=62 printed_page=60 -->

- **(3)** The overture is vague in some of its stipulations. For example, the overture fails to define "a wholly Christian education." Likewise, “financial, spiritual, and instructional assistance" that is “helpful” is vague. The Constitution already stipulates the office of deacon is provided for "helping one another in time of need" (BCO 9-1) and “it is the duty of the deacons to minister to those who are in need" (BCO 9-2).

12. That the General Assembly approve the 2020 CDM budget as presented by the Administrative Committee. Deferred to the CoC on AC

13. That the General Assembly approve the June 2018 minutes of the CDM Permanent Committee meeting. Adopted

III. Recommendations

1. That Overture 3 from Northern New England Presbytery, "Amend RAO 10-3 to Promote the Exercise of Godly Prudence in Planning and Leading Times of Corporate Prayer and Worship at General Assembly," be answered in the negative. Adopted Grounds A protest and point of order were raised at the Forty-sixth General Assembly regarding offenses taken at a pre-assembly prayer meeting (M46GA, 2018, p. 20, Item 46-15 Protest): TE Dwight L. Dolby presented a formal protest regarding the published prayer litany used at the pre-Assembly Prayer Gathering. TE Kevin Twit raised a point of order that the protest was out of order for being intemperate and for calling future Assemblies to action. On advice from the parliamentarians, the Moderator ruled the protest out of order because it was not against an action of the Assembly, [emphasis added] but rather against a pre-Assembly function (BCO 45-3). The ruling on the protest rendered the point of order moot." RAO 10-3 relates to the corporate worship services of the entire General Assembly, not to pre-Assembly prayer meetings. Overture 3 combines public worship services of the entire Assembly with pre-Assembly prayer meetings. The primary function of the AC regarding pre-Assembly prayer meetings is to provide a room for commissioners and guests to pray for the General Assembly. Those involved in pre- Assembly prayer meetings are already expected to use godly prudence and wisdom in conducting such prayer meetings. There were several rooms made available for pre-Assembly prayer meetings in 2018. Some attendees could have taken issue with what was said at any of those gatherings. A better means of dealing with the issue of potential offenses is for leaders of prayer meetings to exercise godly wisdom in leading prayer meetings and for attendees to refrain from making corporate confessions of sin on matters for which they do not individually believe themselves to be culpable. 65

<a id="ga47-p68"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=68 printed_page=66 -->

For AC staff or Committee members to attend, monitor, and report on every potential offense that could be taken by any individual at every pre-Assembly prayer meeting would be impractical.

2. That Overture 11 from Fellowship Presbytery, "Commend and Distribute the RPCNA's 'Contemporary Perspectives on Sexual Orientation: A Theological and Pastoral Analysis," be answered in the negative. Adopted Grounds The report of the Cooperative Ministries Committee already suggested to courts and members of the PCA the RPCNA report as a useful resource (M44GA, 2016, p. 334) along with other resources. There could be some copyright issues involved in printing and distributing the RPCNA report. The RPCNA report is already available for online access to anyone interested as Overture 11 mentions http://rparchives.org/data/Minutes%20of%20 Synod/ 2011%20 Minutes.pdf. Ordinarily the distribution of reports and materials to Presbyteries, Teaching Elders, and Sessions is the responsibility of the AC. The distribution of the RPCNA report would be another unfunded mandate to the AC to distribute the RPCNA to approximately 1,800 churches and 4,800 ministers.

3. That Overture 24 from Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery, “Add Constitutional Precedence Statement to Policy Manuals," be answered in the affirmative as amended as follows: Therefore, it is resolved... to add the following statement as a preface or conclusion to all policy manuals of the Permanent Committees and Agencies: “<del>At every point, this entire</del> <del>manual is subordinate to</del> <del>the entire Constitution of the</del> <del>Presbyterian Church in America the Westminster</del> <del>Standards</del> <del>and the Book of Church Order. If there exists any</del> <del>conflict between the PCA's constitutional</del> <del>documents and</del> <del>the content and stipulations of this manual, the Constitution</del> <del>carries final</del> authority." "The ecclesiastical Constitution of the Church is defined in the Book of Church Order, Preface III. The provisions of the Constitution shall control over any provisions of this policy manual that may be in conflict therewith."

66

<a id="ga47-p69"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=69 printed_page=67 -->

Further resolved, that any material change in a policy manual  
produced <del>or amended-by</del> any of the Permanent Committees  
and Agencies shall, <del>before becoming operational</del>, be  
approved by its respective committee or board and  
submitted to the General Assembly <del>for ratification</del> through  
the usual process of the reports of the Permanent  
Committees and Agencies in accordance with RAO 4-21.j  
and RAO 14-11.d, f, g, h.  
Further resolved that each of the Permanent Committees and  
Agencies <del>report back on the implementation of</del> <del>these actions</del>  
to shall act to include a statement of Constitutional  
Precedence in their respective policy manuals and record  
such action in their minutes and, in this manner, report to  
their respective Committee of Commissioners at the 48th  
General Assembly so that the Committees of Commissioners  
may examine the minutes of Committees and Agencies and  
report to the General Assembly.  
Adopted  
Grounds:  
Our “Corporate Bylaws of the Presbyterian Church in America  
(A Corporation), Article VIII, Section 1" has a statement of  
Constitutional Precedence, “The ecclesiastical Constitution of  
the Church is defined in the Book of Church Order, Preface III.  
The provisions of the Constitution shall control over any  
provisions of these Bylaws that may be in conflict therewith."  
The above recommendation is simply an adaptation of the  
Corporate Bylaws of the Presbyterian Church in America (A  
Corporation), Article VIII, Section 1.  
Robert's Rules of Order prohibits actions or motions that are  
contrary to an entity's constitution, RONR (11th ed.) p. 343, ll.  
14-17. If any such actions or motions are approved, they are  
invalid. In a sense, the overture is unnecessary. Nevertheless, it  
would be appropriate to include a statement regarding the  
priority of the PCA Constitution.  
BCO 14-1.7 ensures that Committees and Agencies do  
not infringe upon the rights or powers of any church court  
(Session, Presbytery, or General Assembly). "The Assembly's  
committees are to serve and not to direct any Church  
judicatories. They are not to establish policy, but rather execute  
policy established by the General Assembly."

67

<a id="ga47-p70"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=70 printed_page=68 -->

BCO 14-1.7 has historically been understood to mean major  
ecclesiastical policies, not every-day-operations policies. For  
example, the MTW Cooperative Agreement with independent  
missions agencies was a major issue at the Second General  
Assembly (M2GA, 1974, pp. 66, 68). The General Assembly,  
however, has never decided every-day-operations policies such  
as the office hours of a Committee or Agency, on which holidays  
offices are to be closed, the salary range of staff persons other  
than the Chief Administrative Officers, staff job descriptions, or  
personnel vacations, etc.  
RAO 4-21.j states that “An up-to-date copy of the bylaws and  
manual of the Committee or Agency, if such exists, should be  
kept with the minutes." A Committee of Commissioners may  
examine those bylaws and manual(s) under RAO 14-11.  
RAO 14-11 provides a procedure in examining the minutes of a  
Committee or Agency for a Committee of Commissioners to  
report to the General Assembly any alleged violations of the  
PCA Constitution, a procedure for the Committee or Agency to  
respond, and a procedure for the General Assembly to decide on  
any exception taken to the minutes.  
Committee or Agency policies are subject to the requirements of  
the civil law. That relates to corporate laws and sexual abuse,  
misconduct, or harassment laws as well.  
There is a difference between employment law and ecclesiastical  
discipline. Each has its own respective procedures and  
requirements. They may be similar, but are not legally or  
ecclesiastically required to be identical. For example, a  
Committee or Agency could terminate an employee for a failure  
adequately to carry out one's responsibilities, which could not  
necessarily be a matter of ecclesiastical discipline. If it were a  
possible matter for ecclesiastical discipline, the Committee or  
Agency should report the matter to the ecclesiastical court of  
original jurisdiction for the ecclesiastical court to make a  
determination in accordance with the Book of Church Order,  
Part II, The Rules of Discipline.  
Committees and Agencies would be well advised to make a  
distinction between policy manuals and handbooks. For  
example, Covenant College could have handbooks that stipulate  
what a minimum or maximum teaching load for a professor  
would be or what expectations of student conduct are, without  
the necessity of getting the General Assembly's approval.  
68

<a id="ga47-p71"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=71 printed_page=69 -->

4. That Overture 27 from Westminster Presbytery, "Study Possibility of Remote Voting at General Assembly," be answered in the negative. <del class="double-strikethrough">with the proviso that the AC report its finding and</del> <del class="double-strikethrough">positive or negative recommendation regarding the feasibility to the</del> <del class="double-strikethrough">Forty eighth General Assembly in 2020</del>. Adopted Grounds: Both creation and redemption highlight the value of humans being embodied creatures. The historic practice at GA of singing Psalm 133 with its distinctively physical images, as well as RAO 1-1 which indicates that the GA begin with a worship service including prayer, a sermon, and the Lord's Supper, recognize the church's physical presence together in one place as being constitutive of the Assembly. Because a technology exists does not mean it should be implemented. As indicated by our cultural moment, conversation on weighty matters involving deeply held theological and religious convictions are best discussed face to face. Engaging important issues in the same room is fundamentally different than over a screen. Implementing Distance Voting runs the risk of communicating to TEs and REs (and to congregants) that being physical present for the work of the church is not essential. As indicated in the Theological Ground, Christian worship is physical in nature. The work of the General Assembly and our church courts goes beyond voting on substantive issues, but glorifying God and edifying one another as the body of Christ. The primary concern of Overture 27 is the involvement of REs in the work of the GA. However, no supportive data is given that indicates that proxy voting would increase RE involvement. The overture does not have a specific cost and cap of implementing a new technology. Currently the AC does not have appropriate cyber security policies in place for implementation of a distributive service (i.e. cloud service).

47-39 Overtures Committee Report TE Bruce O'Neil made a procedural motion that the Assembly take up Overture 42 first in the Overture Committee Report. Overtures Committee Chairman TE Sean Lucas explained the Committee's rationale for the order in which they were presenting the overtures. After a short debate, a motion to call the question passed. The procedural motion failed (355- 880) Chairman Lucas led the Assembly in prayer and presented the report (see p. 86). TE Lucas brought before the Assembly the overtures dealing with changes to the BCO, explaining the Committee's rationale for each recommendation. He then moved in gross Recommendations 17, 36, 1, 5, 9, and 34 related to the corresponding Overtures. Upon request, Overture 9 was removed from the in gross motion. Recommendations 17, 36, 1, 5, and 34, regarding the corresponding overtures, were adopted in gross. by voice vote. Recommendation 9 to answer Overture 9 in the affirmative as amended by the CoC was adopted by voice vote. Recommendation 33 to answer Overture 33 in the negative was adopted by voice vote. Chairman Lucas proceeded to consideration of the overtures regarding human sexuality (Overtures 4, 22, 11, 35, 39, 42, 30, 44, 45, 37, and 28). RE Mel Duncan presented the Committee's Recommendation 4 that Overture 4 (to declare the “Nashville Statement’ on Biblical Sexuality as a Biblically Faithful Declaration") be answered in the affirmative. A Minority Report for Recommendation 4 (see p. 112), presented by RE Jim Wert, offered a substitute motion that Overture 4 be recommitted to the Overtures Committee of the 48th General Assembly. RE Duncan responded on behalf of the OC. Debate on the issue ensued. RE Duncan gave the final word for the Committee's recommendation.(RAO 19-4.b). The Minority Report calling for recommittal of Overture 4 failed (572-792). Recommendation 4 that Overture 4 be answered in affirmative was adopted (803-541).

76

<a id="ga47-p79"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=79 printed_page=77 -->

Recommendation 22 that Overture 22 be answered with reference to answer to Overture 4 was adopted by voice vote. Chairman Lucas presented Recommendation 11, that Overture 11 be answered in the affirmative as amended by the CoC. According to a previous motion of the Assembly, the Moderator offered the privilege of the floor to representatives of AC, CDM, CC, and RUF, to whom the Overture had also been referred. As no representative came forward to speak, the Moderator called for a vote, and Recommendation 11 was adopted by voice vote. Recommendation 35, that Overture 35 be ruled out of order by the Moderator (RONR (11th ed.) p. 104 ll. 24-31), was so ruled on the grounds given in the OC Report (p. 103). Recommendation 39, that Overture 39 be ruled out of order by the Moderator (RONR (11th ed.) p. 104 ll. 24-31), was so ruled on the grounds given in the OC Report (p. 691). Chairman Lucas presented Recommendation 42, that Overture 42, “Establish Study Committee on Sexuality," be answered in the affirmative as amended by the CoC. [Clerk's Note: The Assembly adopted the Administrative Committee CoC changes to the overture recommending that the budget for the Study Committee be raised from $15,000 to $25,000, provided solely by designated gifts to the AC (p. 70).] After a short debate, a motion to call the question passed (1216-85). Recommendation 42 was adopted by voice vote. Recommendations 30, 44, and 45, that Overtures 30, 44, and 45 be answered with reference to overture 42, were moved in gross. Seeing no opposition, the Moderator declared them adopted by common consent. Recommendation 37, that Overture 37, “Assembly Statement on Same-sex Attraction," be answered with reference to Assembly's answer to Overture 4, was presented. A Minority Report for Recommendation 37 (see p. 134) offered a substitute motion that Overture 37, as amended by the Minority, be answered in the affirmative. In accordance with RAO 15-8 g (1), TE Sean Lucas, Chairman, presented the committee's rationale. TE Daniel Shrock presented the Minority Report. TE Sean Lucas then gave a response. Debate on the floor ensued. A motion to call the question passed by hand vote. The substitute motion of the Minority failed (492-724) Recommendation 37, that Overture 37 be answered with reference to Overture 4, was adopted by common consent.

77

TE Sean Lucas, Chairman, presented the committee's rationale for its recommendation. TE Steve Warhurst presented the Minority Report. TE David Richter rose to a point of order that the Minority Report was not appropriate because an argument being made was not germane to the overture. The Moderator ruled that the point of order was well taken and that the line of argument was not germane to the overture. TE Warhurst challenged the ruling of the chair. The Moderator ruled the point of order was not well taken because the Revoice conference was mentioned in the overture, and he allowed TE Warhurst to continue. The question was called, and the substitute motion of the Minority failed (210-967) Hearing no objection, the Moderator declared that Recommendation 28 was adopted by common consent, thereby answering Overture 28 with reference to Overture 4. ### IV. Recommendations

1. That Overture 1 from Northwest Georgia Presbytery (“Revise BCO 14-2 to Permit Additional Ruling Elder Representation at the General Assembly," p. 581) be answered in the negative. Adopted

<a id="ga47-p90"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=90 printed_page=88 -->

Grounds: The Overture points out the continuing imbalance between Teaching and Ruling Elder attendance at General Assembly but will not solve the problem it purports to address. Because many PCA churches send no Ruling Elders to the Assembly, simply increasing the number of Ruling Elders a church may send will not have a significant effect.

2. That Overture 2 from Northwest Georgia Presbytery (“Encourage CTS toward Growth and Release from Assembly Oversight," p. 584) be answered in the negative. Adopted

Grounds: The overture is worded in a way that suggests that the Seminary wants to leave the denomination, but this is not the case. The seminary board has stated, as the overtures committee heard from President Dalbey, that Covenant Seminary emphatically does not want to be removed from denominational oversight and, in fact, greatly appreciates all the advantages and accountability that denominational connection and oversight provides. Covenant Seminary was received into the PCA as a part of Joining and Receiving and it remaining as a part of the denomination is a part of the commitments that were made at Joining and Receiving. Covenant Seminary, as reported by President Dalbey, does not desire to have unordained persons serving as members of its board. All board members must affirm agreement with the Westminster Standards once a year. Every faculty member must also affirm agreement with the Westminster Standards yearly. Every faculty member is approved by a vote of the CTS board, which is nominated and elected by the General Assembly of the PCA. The president of Covenant Seminary has passed examination by the GA's Theological Examining Committee While members of the Overtures Committee are very appreciative of all our confessional seminaries, having a denominational seminary is a great blessing and benefit to the Presbyterian Church in America.

88

<a id="ga47-p91"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=91 printed_page=89 -->

3. [Overture 3 (p. 587) was referred by the Stated Clerk to AC.]

4. That Overture 4 from Calvary Presbytery (“Declare the Council on Biblical Manhood & Womanhood's ‘Nashville Statement’ on Biblical Sexuality as a Biblically Faithful Declaration," p. 589) be answered in the affirmative. Adopted

Grounds: This Overture commends the Nashville Statement as a useful, faithful, accurate, and careful summary of biblical truth. This Overture instructs the PCA to do what our Book of Church Order instructs us to do: "minister and declare" God's truth to God's people. This overture is also very simple and clear. It's an excellent resource that every Sunday school teacher, elder, deacon, member of the PCA can read, understand, and apply in ministry and conversation. Lastly this Overture is necessary. It appears that many commissioners have come to Dallas concerned about the discussion of sexuality within the PCA. This Overture sends a strong word that the PCA loves people struggling with same-sex attraction so much that we are willing to tell them careful, faithful, biblical teaching on sexuality.

5. That Overture 5 from Central Indiana Presbytery (“Amend BCO 23-1 on Procedures for Dissolving Various Pastoral Relations,"

- **p.** 583) be referred back to Central Indiana Presbytery without prejudice. Adopted

Grounds: The Overture does not adequately resolve all the issues it addresses and is in need of further refinement to be consistent with other sections of the BCO. The best mechanism for further refinement is to have the presbytery submit a revised version in the future.

6. That Overture 6 from Pacific Northwest Presbytery (“Amend RAO 11 and 13 to Disallow Memorials," p. 594) be answered in the affirmative [See Partial OC Report, p. 24]. Adopted

8. That Overture 8 from Ohio Valley Presbytery (“Amend BCO 14-1.10, 14-1.11, and 14-1.12 to Allow Non-ordained Persons to serve on Committees and Boards," p. 601) be answered in the negative.

Adopted

Grounds: This Overture would allow non-ordained men or women, who have not taken a vow to uphold our Constitution, to have a part in the governance of the church. Such persons may usefully serve as giving information and advice, but they, apart from Constitutional commitment, should not be part of the decision-making process itself. Further, a substantially similar overture was rejected by the 46th Assembly. The arguments have not changed or become more persuasive.

Adopted Therefore, be it resolved, that the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America amend BCO 32-8, 32-13 and 35-10 with the following (additions are underlined, deletions are struck through): 32-8. When the offense with which an accused person stands charged took place at a distance, <del>and</del> and it

99

<a id="ga47-p102"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=102 printed_page=100 -->

is inconvenient for the witnesses to appear before the  
court having jurisdiction, that court may either (a)  
appoint a commission of its body, or (b) request the  
coordinate court contiguous to the place where the  
facts occurred, to take the testimony for it, or (c) have  
the testimony taken by videoconference, which shall  
employ technical means that ensure that all persons  
participating in the meeting can see and hear each  
other at the same time, and which allows for live  
cross-examination by both parties. The accused shall  
always have reasonable notice of the time and place  
of the meeting of this commission or coordinate court.

32-13. In order that the trial may be fair and impartial, the witnesses shall be examined in the presence of the accused (as permitted by BCO 32-8), or at least after he shall have received due citation to attend. Witnesses may be cross-examined by both parties, and any questions asked must be pertinent to the issue.

35-10. When it is not convenient for a court to have  
the whole or perhaps any part of the testimony in any  
particular case taken in its presence, a commission  
shall be appointed, or coordinate court requested, to  
take the testimony in question, which shall be  
considered as if taken in the presence of the court.

Due notice of the commission or coordinate court or  
videoconference, and of the time and place of its  
meeting, shall be given to the opposite party, that he  
may have an opportunity of attending. If the accused  
shall desire on his part to take testimony at a distance  
for his own exculpation, he shall give notice to the  
court of the time and place at which it shall be taken,  
in order that a commission or coordinate court, as in  
the former case, may be appointed for the purpose.  
Testimony may be taken on written interrogatories by  
filing the same with the clerk of the court having  
jurisdiction of the case, and giving two weeks' notice  
thereof to the adverse party, during which time he

<a id="ga47-p103"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=103 printed_page=101 -->

may file cross-interrogatories, if he desire it. Testimony  
shall then be taken by the commission or coordinate  
court in answer to the direct and cross-interrogatories,  
if such are filed, and no notice need be given of the  
time and place of taking the testimony.

Grounds: The Overture gives courts the option to use modern  
technology to take testimony from witnesses, in addition to creating  
a commission or using a coordinate court. The amendments to this  
overture address the concerns of CCB about consistency in  
application in two other sections of the BCO.

Adopted Therefore, be it resolved that the 47th General Assembly create an Ad-Interim Committee (AIC) to study the topic of human sexuality with particular attention to the issues of homosexuality, same-sex attraction, and transgenderism, and prepare a report which:

Shall include an annotated bibliography of resources on sexuality which the Committee endorses to help pastors and sessions shepherd congregants who are dealing with same-sex attraction; and Shall address: (1) the nature of temptation, sin, <del class="double-strikethrough">and</del> repentance, and the difference between Roman Catholic and Reformed views of concupiscence as regards same sex- attraction; (2) the propriety of using terms like “gay Christian” when referring to a believer struggling with same-sex attraction; (3) the status of "orientation" as a valid anthropological category; (4) the practice of "spiritual friendship" among same sex attracted Christians; and

104

<a id="ga47-p107"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=107 printed_page=105 -->

Shall include an analysis of WLC 138 and 139 regarding same-sex attraction, with careful attention given to the compatibility of the 7th commandment and same-sex attraction and the pursuit of celibacy by those who are attracted to the same sex, and Shall include exegesis of the terms "malakoi" and "arsenokoitai" (1 Cor. 6:9); and Shall include suggested ways to articulate and defend a Biblical understanding of homosexuality, same sex-attraction, and transgenderism in the context of a culture that denies that understanding; and Should the Committee conclude it prudent, may, as one of its recommendations, propose a statement on the topic; and

Be it further resolved, that, in its examination of Scripture and the PCA of Faith and Catechisms, the Committee consider studies and statements of other bodies outside and within the PCA (including, but not limited to, the Council on Biblical Manhood and Womanhood's “Nashville Statement"; the RPCNA's “Contemporary Confession Perspectives on Sexual Orientation: A Theological and Pastoral Analysis"; the RPCES’ "Pastoral Care for the Repentant Homosexual"; Missouri Presbytery's "Homosexuality and the Gospel of Grace: Faithfulness to the Lord's Calling in an Age of Sexual Autonomy"; the Central Carolina Presbytery Study Committee Report on 2018 Revoice Conference; the 2019 Missouri Presbytery Report on the Revoice Conference; the statements on homosexuality issued by the 5th, 24th, and 27th General Assemblies of the PCA and the January 14, 2015, Report of the CMC Subcommittee on Homosexuality) and resources recommended in those documents; and

Be it further resolved that the Moderator of the 47th General Assembly appoint the seven voting members who shall be either PCA teaching or PCA ruling elders, and the Committee shall include at least <del class="double-strikethrough">twe</del> three teaching and <del class="double-strikethrough">two</del> three ruling elders <del class="double-strikethrough">including members whose writings</del> <del class="double-strikethrough">reflect theological engagement on the issue and pastoral</del> 105

<a id="ga47-p108"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=108 printed_page=106 -->

<del class="double-strikethrough">interaction with those dealing with same sex attraction and</del> <del class="double-strikethrough">transgenderism</del>; and

Be it further resolved that the Committee be permitted to recruit others to serve the Committee as advisors within the confines of its budget, with particular concern to secure advisors with experience in counseling those dealing with same-sex attraction and transgenderism; and

Be it further resolved that the budget for the study committee be set at $15,000/year and that funds be derived from gifts to the AC designated for that purpose; and

Be it further resolved that the committee shall present its report to the 48th General Assembly, including any recommendations it may present.

*<del class="double-strikethrough">The Ohio presbytery version here reads "that in addition</del> <del class="double-strikethrough">to Scripture and the PCA Confession of Faith and</del> <del class="double-strikethrough">Catechisms...." Trinity's Session made the small</del> <del class="double-strikethrough">amendment to "in its examination of</del>..."

Grounds: As of today, the PCA is not unified in how it should respond to present-day controversies surrounding human sexuality. While there is little, if any, debate within the PCA over the Scripture's teaching on sexual immorality, there are differences in what written statements we should make about it as a denomination. In cases of such controversy, a study committee is helpful in clarifying what all perspectives can affirm while articulating the more controversial views with nuance and sensitivity. While there is considerable consensus among presbyters on the Biblical doctrine of human sexuality, there are different opinions on how best to pastor those struggling with homosexual sin and temptation. A study committee provides the opportunity to offer guidance and resources on such counseling. Different presbyteries have proposed different statements of affirmation and denials regarding human sexuality, each emphasizing different aspects of the denomination's response to

106

<a id="ga47-p109"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=109 printed_page=107 -->

the issues. The different views coming from the different presbyteries should be studied and resolved. None of the statements recommended by the overtures committee include all of the pious advice that our churches and ministers are requesting. A study committee is a time-honored way to present a unified and consistent report and advice regarding these issues.

### OVERTURES COMMITTEE

### MINORITY REPORTS (OVERTURES 4, 8, 28, 37)

### MINORITY REPORT – OVERTURE 4

If Overture 42 has been answered in the affirmative prior to this report, then the minority will bring the following substitute motion:

Substitute Motion: That Overture 4 be answered in reference to the Assembly's action on Overture 42.

If this report comes to the floor prior to Overture 42, then the minority will bring the following substitute: [Clerk's Note: Overture 4 was adopted before Overture 42 was taken up.]

Substitute Motion: That Overture 4 from Calvary Presbytery recommitted to the Overtures Committee of the 48th General Assembly.

Rationale:

1. The minority believes that the Nashville Statement should be a part of the material studied by a General Assembly Study Committee. A study committee is a far better way to make a clear and decisive statement on the urgent issue of human sexuality.

2. Overture 4 only asks the Assembly to "declare...the 'Nashville Statement'... as a biblically faithful declaration." It does not make it an official document of the PCA. We need a stronger statement by our denomination and a study committee can do this. A study 112

<a id="ga47-p115"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=115 printed_page=113 -->

committee report would be a part of our official documents given to all of our presbyteries, churches, and ministers as pious advice. We need such a resource as a study committee made up of some of our best can produce.

3. The Nashville Statement does not address the issue of pastoral care. Our denomination needs a strong biblical, theological, and pastoral statement on this topic.

Signed

Grounds:

We believe that this overture affirms the gifts that have been distributed to the saints in the Church, (Romans 12:4-8, I Corinthians 12: 4-31) while affirming the “spiritual commonwealth” (BCO 3-1) in which members elect godly men to be ordained as elders who are given the power of jurisdiction as they act jointly in the courts of the church. (BCO 3-2).

Approving this overture will not place non-ordained men and women in  
positions of authority that is to be reserved exclusively for ordained men.  
This overture allows for non-ordained men and women to serve on the  
committees of the church. It is important to add emphasis to the word  
committee. Unlike commissions, committees are appointed by courts and are  
limited in that they are only permitted “to examine, consider, and report' to  
their constituting court regarding the matters that the court delegates to them  
(BCO 15-1). They do not exercise governing authority. The Permanent  
Committees of the General Assembly are subject to additional Constitutional  
constraint in that they are established "to serve and not direct any Church  
judicatories. They are not to establish policy, but rather execute policy  
established by the General Assembly". (BCO 14-1.7)

This overture is written to give confidence that the non-ordained men and women that are placed in nomination for service on these committees are

118

<a id="ga47-p121"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=121 printed_page=119 -->

qualified to serve. Each candidate must first be a member in good standing. All members in good standing are accountable to their sessions having taken a vow to submit themselves “to the government and discipline of the church” (BCO 57.5). Additionally, each candidate will be required to get an endorsement from their session that gives testimony to the nominee's Christian character, their knowledge of and assent to the Constitution of the Church and their promise of faithful service to the General Assembly. Just as our courts serve the Church well by training, examining and holding officers accountable, we anticipate that sessions and presbyteries will be diligent in preparing, examining and holding accountable those that will be nominated and chosen to serve the General Assembly.

Finally, we would note the conflict with the RAO that would be created were this overture to be approved. However, the RAO is subordinate to the BCO and any conflicts would be resolved in favor of the BCO. Further, if the overture is approved, subsequent assemblies can approve changes to the RAO that would bring the RAO into compliance with the BCO.

In summary, this overture will demonstrates our high view of complementarianism by recognizing the gifts and abilities of all of our members, men and women, while avoiding the errors of egalitarianism by correctly assigning distinct roles and responsibilities to the ordained officers of the church.

We would respectfully urge the commissioners of the 47th General Assembly to answer this overture in the affirmative.

Romans 7:22-23 For I delight in the law of God according to the inward man. 23 But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members. Those who delight in the law of God have a sinful nature that is warring against the new nature. They not only have unwanted desires but do things they do not want to do at some level. The presence of unwanted attractions is part of the Christian experience, but it is wrong to deduce that these affections and inclinations are natural, neutral, or good, when God condemns them. Galatians 5:16-17 I say then: Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh. 17 For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, so that you do not do the things that you wish. No doubt this war between the flesh and the spirit makes us wretched, and our only hope is to turn to the Lord Jesus who alone can deliver us from what Paul calls the law of sin. 125

<a id="ga47-p128"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=128 printed_page=126 -->

Romans 7:24-25 O wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? 25 I thank God--through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, with the mind I myself serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin.

Article 7 WE AFFIRM that Christians ought to abhor homosexual sin. Abhorrence of all sin should be cultivated. The fear of the Lord is to hate evil. Leviticus 18:22 You shall not lie with a male as with a woman. It is an abomination. If God abhors something, then His people should abhor it as well. He calls sodomy an abomination, so we should see it as abominable. Psalm 97:10 You who love the LORD, hate evil! God calls us to hate all sin, particularly sexual sin. We should abhor all sexual sin including adultery (Lev.18:20), incest (Lev.18:6), and bestiality (Lev.18:23). WE DENY that revulsion and abhorrence of homosexual sin is sinful. Romans 12:9 Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor what is evil. Cling to what is good. Christians are not called to overlook evil or redefine it. The one who loves without hypocrisy abhors what is evil and clings to what is good. 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 Love suffers long and is kind; love does not envy; love does not parade itself, is not puffed up; 5 does not behave rudely, does not seek its own, is not provoked, thinks no evil; 6 does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices in the truth; 7 bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Those who rejoice in and celebrate ‘homosexual love’ are rejoicing in iniquity. This is not love as the Bible defines it. Love for those in sin means abhorring their sin. Love is patient and kind and does not behave rudely. Love does not seek its selfish interests but rejoices in the truth, including the truth that God hates sexual sin.

Article 8 WE AFFIRM that people living in homosexual sin should be shown kindness and lovingly encouraged to turn from their sin to serve Christ who alone can deliver them from sin and its shame. Mark 2:16-17 And when the scribes and Pharisees saw Him eating with the tax collectors and sinners, they said to His disciples, "How is it that He eats

<a id="ga47-p129"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=129 printed_page=127 -->

and drinks with tax collectors and sinners?" 17 When Jesus heard it, He said to them, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance." Jesus ate and drank with sinners. He loved them by calling them to repentance. This loving call to repentance is not only for those outside the church but also for those inside the church who have strayed. James 5:19-20 Brethren, if anyone among you wanders from the truth, and someone turns him back, 20 let him know that he who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death and cover a multitude of sins. 2 Timothy 2:24-26 And a servant of the Lord must not quarrel but be gentle to all, able to teach, patient, 25 in humility correcting those who are in opposition, if God perhaps will grant them repentance, so that they may know the truth, 26 and that they may come to their senses and escape the snare of the devil, having been taken captive by him to do his will. WE DENY that it is loving or kind to try to diminish or remove the shame of homosexual attraction and orientation, since God calls it shameful. Homosexual attractions and the acts they desire are shameful. Romans 1:26-27 For this reason God gave them up to vile passions. For even their women exchanged the natural use for what is against nature. 27 Likewise also the men, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their lust for one another, men with men committing what is shameful, and receiving in themselves the penalty of their error which was due. It is right to blush and be ashamed of abominations. Shame for sin is a means of grace that leads us to repentance. It is right to have deep and painful shame for all sins and flee to Christ for cleansing. When teachers try to remove the shame of sin or diminish the shame apart from Christ, they are cruel teachers. Jeremiah 6:14-15 They have also healed the hurt of My people slightly, Saying, 'Peace, peace!' When there is no peace. 15 Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? No! They were not at all ashamed; Nor did they know how to blush. Therefore they shall fall among those who fall; At the time I punish them, They shall be cast down," says the LORD. We should weep for those who glory in their sin. Philippians 3:18-19 For many walk, of whom I have told you often, and now tell you even weeping, that they are the enemies of the cross of Christ: 19 whose end is destruction, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame--who set their mind on earthly things.

127

<a id="ga47-p130"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=130 printed_page=128 -->

The faithful friend rebukes sin and encourages blushing for sin. Sinners should be ashamed of their sins which lead to death and submit to God who alone removes the shame of sin. Any attempt to remove shame some other way is wicked. Romans 6:21-23 What fruit did you have then in the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. 22 But now having been set free from sin, and having become slaves of God, you have your fruit to holiness, and the end, everlasting life. 23 For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. When God gives a sinner the ability to blush for their sin and fear the death it brings, this is grace. In Christ, we are set free from sin and made slaves to God who alone gives us eternal life. To coddle sin is death. To forsake it and cling to Christ is eternal life. If a man has a deadly disease and you have the cure, then you must tell him of his disease and offer him the cure. You must persuade him of the deadly nature of his disease. It would be wicked to say, “Your fine, your fine," when he is dying. The first step to escaping abominable sin is to acknowledge that it is an abomination. It is right to be ashamed of sin and blush for it. It is good to turn from it to Christ who alone can take away the shame of our sin.

Article 9 WE AFFIRM that repentant sinners turning from all unnatural attractions and trusting in Christ should be welcomed into the church as members in good standing. 1 Timothy 1:15-16 This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief. 16 However, for this reason I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might show all longsuffering, as a pattern to those who are going to believe on Him for everlasting life. Christ saves sinners. Some people are greater sinners than others, but God saved the chief sinner—the Apostle Paul—as a pattern to those who are going to believe on Him for everlasting life. Thus, repentant sinners turning from abominable sins to trust in Christ Jesus, the Savior of sinners, should be welcomed into the church with open arms. WE DENY that followers of Christ who struggle with homosexual attraction should be identified as “LGBT+ Christians," because it dishonors Christ to identify with sinful attractions and orientations. 1 Corinthians 6:9-11 Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived; neither fornicators, nor idolaters, 128

nor adulterers, nor effeminate, nor homosexuals, 10 nor thieves, nor the covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers, will inherit the kingdom of God. 11 Such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God. (NASB) If a person practices fornication, idolatry, adultery, homosexuality, or drunkenness, then they are rightly labeled fornicators, idolaters, adulterers, homosexuals, or drunkards. If, however, they forsake these sins and turn to the Lord Jesus Christ, and by the power of His Spirit try to put to death these sinful thoughts, words, and deeds, then they no longer deserve these labels. They are washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God. To label them with the degrading name of fornicator, drunkard, or homosexual is an insult to Christ who has set them apart for Himself. 2 Corinthians 5:16-17 Therefore, from now on, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know Him thus no longer. 17 Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new. We are new creations in Christ. Something is wrong if we want to identify with those things which are shameful and brought death to us. Romans 6:21-23 What fruit did you have then in the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. 22 But now having been set free from sin, and having become slaves of God, you have your fruit to holiness, and the end, everlasting life. 23 For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. I fear that some who identify as ‘Gay Christians’ do not understand the shame of their sin. They still want to glory in what is shameful. The entire culture around us is glorying in this sin and celebrating this sin. The homosexual must learn to be ashamed of the sin and flee to Christ. Those who understand the shame of their idolatry, adultery, drunkenness, and fornication do not want to identify as “Idolatrous Christians” or “Drunken Christians” or “Incestuous Christians.” The man who still struggles with lust for women other than his wife does not want to identify as an “Adulterous Christian." Why is homosexuality a special sin that deserves recognition? We fear it may be the first steps toward the acceptance of homosexuality in the PCA. See the article:

“The Overhauling of Straight America” by Marshall Kirk and Erastes Pill (a pen name—an erastes was a man in Greek culture that pursued adolescent boys)

Article 10 WE AFFIRM that homosexual attraction should be mortified by the power of the Spirit. Colossians 3:5-7 Therefore put to death your members which are on the earth: fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry. 6 Because of these things the wrath of God is coming upon the sons of disobedience, 7 in which you yourselves once walked when you lived in them. All evil passions and desires should be put to death. Homosexual passions are evil (Rom.1:24-27) and need to be mortified by the Spirit. Romans 8:12-14 Therefore, brethren, we are debtors--not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. 13 For if you live according to the flesh you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. 14 For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God. All sexual immorality in thought, word, or deed is to be avoided. We are to control our bodies in sanctification and live honorable lives, free from the passion of lust that dominates the culture of unbelievers. 1 Thessalonians 4:3-5 For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you should abstain from sexual immorality; 4 that each of you should know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, 5 not in passion of lust, like the Gentiles who do not know God; WE DENY that continuing homosexual attraction or failure to attain orientation change is evidence of God's approval of these unnatural and vile passions. Romans 7:21-25 I find then a law, that evil is present with me, the one who wills to do good. 22 For I delight in the law of God according to the inward man. 23 But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members. 24 O wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? 25 I thank God--through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, with the mind I myself serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin. Many Christians struggle with unwanted attractions and war against them for their entire lives; continuing to struggle with sin is never evidence of God's approval of that sin. Christians men struggle with lust 130

for women, desire for pornography, covetousness, and more. These struggles may continue until glorification, but by God's grace can be mortified. Romans 8:12-13 Therefore, brethren, we are debtors--not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. 13 For if you live according to the flesh you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.

Article 11 WE AFFIRM that those struggling with unlawful sexual attractions of any kind should be encouraged to seek the help, prayer, and counsel of mature believers, elders, and pastors. God tells us to confess sins to one another and pray for one another, that God might heal us. Sin should particularly be confessed to righteous men who will pray for us and counsel us. James 5:16 Confess your trespasses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The effective, fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much. We need encouragement in the war against sin. We need daily biblical exhortation so we are not hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. We also need the assembly of the saints. Hebrews 3:12-13 Beware, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief in departing from the living God; 13 but exhort one another daily, while it is called "TODAY," lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. Hebrews 10:24-25 And let us consider one another in order to stir up love and good works, 25 not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as is the manner of some, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching. WE DENY that those struggling with homosexual attraction and orientation should suffer in silence. God has placed believers in the body of Christ so that we might bear one another's burdens. Not only should those struggling with sin break the silence and seek help from others, those who are spiritual should seek out and help those struggling with sin.

Galatians 6:1-2 Brethren, if a man is overtaken in any trespass, you who are spiritual restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you also be tempted. 2 Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ. The church should be a place where sinners get help to overcome their sins.

Article 12 WE AFFIRM that our inward self-conception and outward gender identity must conform to the sex God assigned us at conception, and thus we are to live in obedience to his call evident in our reproductive organs. 1 Corinthians 16:13 Be on the alert, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Men are called to act like men. They are to take responsibility, stand firm, be strong, and defend the weak. They are not to dress like or act like women. Soft or effeminate men (μαλakoì) are excluded from the kingdom of God. 1 Corinthians 6:9-11 Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived; neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor effeminate, nor homosexuals, 10 nor thieves, nor the covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers, will inherit the kingdom of God. 11 Such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God. (NASB) Here, Paul uses the word malakoi, literally meaning “soft ones." In his day, μαλαkoì figuratively meant effeminate. Expositing 1 Corinthians 6:9, Calvin writes, “By effeminate persons I understand those who, although they do not openly abandon themselves to impurity, discover, nevertheless, their unchastity by blandishments of speech, by lightness of gesture and apparel, and other allurements." 1 Corinthians 6:9 does not simply condemn the µαλαkoì when he plays the woman in sodomy, but when he acts like a woman outside the bedroom. The effeminate man rejects God's call for biological males to act like men. Women are to be feminine; they are not to dress or act like men. This is an abomination. Deuteronomy 22:5 "A woman shall not wear man's clothing, nor shall a man put on a woman's clothing; for whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD your God.

132

<a id="ga47-p135"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=135 printed_page=133 -->

WE DENY that physical anomalies or psychological conditions nullify the union God has decreed between biological sex and self-conception and gender identity. The fact that there are people with physical anomalies in their sex organs does not prove that gender is fluid for all people, or that they can identify and act as whatever gender they please. Matthew 19:12 "For there are eunuchs who were born that way from their mother's womb; and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men; and there are also eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. He who is able to accept this, let him accept it." Those born with a physical disorder of sex development are created in the image of God and have dignity and worth equal to all other imagebearers. They are acknowledged by our Lord Jesus in his words about “eunuchs who were born that way from their mother's womb." With all others they are welcome as faithful followers of Jesus Christ and should embrace their biological sex insofar as it may be known. Isaiah 56:3-5 Do not let the son of the foreigner Who has joined himself to the LORD Speak, saying, "The LORD has utterly separated me from His people"; Nor let the eunuch say, "Here I am, a dry tree." 4 For thus says the LORD: "To the eunuchs who keep My Sabbaths, And choose what pleases Me, And hold fast My covenant, 5 Even to them I will give in My house And within My walls a place and a name Better than that of sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name That shall not be cut off. People with ambiguities related to their biological sex can turn from their sins unto Christ and live a fruitful life in joyful obedience to Christ, embracing their biological sex insofar as it is known.

### MINORITY REPORT – OVERTURE 37

We the undersigned recommend that the 47th GA affirm Overture 37 as amended below, affirming that:

1. All human beings are created in God's image, endowed with dignity and purpose to the glory of their Maker (Gen 1:26–27, 9:6; James 3:9).

2. Some Christians and churches regrettably have not loved, listened to, or cared for those experiencing same sex attractions or gender confusion in a manner befitting their identity as God's image bearers or, in the case of believers, as our brothers and sisters in Christ; and we exhort such Christians and churches to repent of these failures.

3. All human beings descending from Adam by ordinary generation are born sinners, having inherited both imputed guilt and enslaving corruption from Adam, and justly deserve God's judgment and wrath (Rom 5:12; Eph 2:1-3).

4. By his death and resurrection Christ has not only procured the justification of his saints whereby they are forgiven and declared righteous in God's sight, but has also secured their freedom from enslavement to sin so that they are able to die unto sin and live unto righteousness in Him (Rom 5:12–19, 6:1-14; Col 3:5-11).

5. When the Spirit unites sinners to Christ by faith, Christ pardons and subdues the corruption of their nature by his grace and grows them in holiness as they work out their salvation with fear and trembling (Phil 2:12–13).

6. Even after such union with Christ, there remains a corruption of their nature that continues to generate all manner of sinful desires, such as anger, disobedience, pride, hatred, lusts, or unnatural sexual attractions (Eph 2:1-3).

7. While external temptations from Satan and the world are not sinful for those subjected to them, internal desires that arise from the corruption of the flesh, including romantic or sexual attraction to a member of the same sex, are sinful and must be pardoned and mortified in Christ (Heb 4:13; John 3:6).

8. The notion that unnatural sexual desires, due to the fall, are merely “disordered” but not sinful, conflicts with the biblical and Reformed doctrine that both the corruption of our nature itself, and all the motions thereof, are truly and properly sin (Rom 7:5-8, 25; Gal 5:17; WCF 6.5).

9. Terms such as "gay Christian," "same-sex attracted Christian," “alcoholic Christian,” “lustful Christian,” “greedy Christian,” etc., do not rightly define the identity of believers; rather, Christians must consider themselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ, in whom they find their identity (Rom 6:11; 1 Cor. 6:9-11). 134

<a id="ga47-p137"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=137 printed_page=135 -->

10. Sanctification is not fully realized in this life, and the remnants of corruption remain in every part of the Christian, which remnants prompt an irreconcilable war between the flesh and the Spirit, such that the Church should never promise the complete removal of sinful desires, including same sex attraction (1 John 1:8; James 3:2; Gal 5:17).

11. Same-sex attraction, spontaneously arising from a Christian's remaining corruption, differs from sin in which a desire is not only conceived in the heart, but breaks forth into action, and those Christians who resist and refuse to act upon such spontaneous attractions in word, thought, and deed are actively mortifying sin in obedience to Christ (1 Cor 10:13; Col

### 3:5; WCF 6.5; WLC 151).

12. The progressive character of sanctification in this life should lead the church to welcome, love, and care for suffering sinners, including those who struggle with same sex attraction and gender confusion, tenderly shepherding them to rest in Christ and walk increasingly in newness of life (1 Thess 5:14; 2 Tim 4:2; Rom 6:4).

13. No temptation has overtaken anyone that is not common to man, so the Church must avoid being a place where those who struggle with same sex attraction and gender confusion are alienated, but rather serve as a haven for sinners who are loved and encouraged to battle against indwelling sin in the covenant community (1 Cor 10:13; Heb 10:25).

Grounds: Overture 37 provided a concise, biblically- and confessionallygrounded explanation of what we believe about the sexual and gender challenges facing our churches. This amended version does the same, tailoring and applying our confessional commitments to the main issues at hand. These affirmations complement in necessary ways the broader truths expressed by the Nashville Statement, offer a faithful framework for any additional study of these issues by a committee, and provide an immediate and sensitive response from the 47th General Assembly to the common concerns of our church.

### FORTY-SEVENTH GENERAL ASSEMBLY

### REFERENCE OF OVERTURES

I refer overtures in accordance with the Rules of Assembly Operations 3-2.g, and Article XI.

### PRESBYTERY VOTES ON THE BOOK OF CHURCH ORDER

### AMENDMENTS

BCO 26-2 requires an affirmative vote of two-thirds of the Presbyteries as part of the amendment process. The seven items originally sent down for vote by the Forty-sixth General Assembly require the affirmative vote of fifty-nine Presbyteries. As of January 1, 2019, we have eighty-eight presbyteries, including West Hudson Presbytery, which was formed out of New York Metropolitan Presbytery.

As of June 7, 2019, all of the seven proposed BCO amendments initially approved by the 46th General Assembly had received the affirmative vote of 59 (2/3) of the presbyteries. A total of 80 presbyteries had recorded their vote with the Stated Clerk's office. Since all of the proposed amendments to the BCO have received the affirmative vote of at least 59 presbyteries prior to the General Assembly, all seven items are before this General Assembly for final vote.

139

<a id="ga47-p142"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=142 printed_page=140 -->

Presbytery Votes on Amendment Sent Down by 46th General Assembly (as of June 7, 2019)

Amend: For Against Item 1 BCO 8-1, 8-3 74 6 Item 2 BCO 25-11 71 9 Item 3 BCO 30-1 63 17 Item 4 BCO 30-3 76 4 Item 5 BCO 32-19 64 16 Item 6 BCO 35-11 67 13 Item 7 BCO 59-3 77 3

For a complete tally of the presbytery votes as of June 7, please see Attachment, p. 150.

Presbyteries need to be aware that not voting on a proposed amendment to the BCO is tantamount to a negative vote (BCO 26-2) because the advice and consent of two-thirds of Presbyteries are required. That is unlike Robert's Rules of Order in which abstentions (refraining to vote) are not counted in determining a majority. The BCO is of higher parliamentary authority than Robert’s Rules of Order.
