### PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA FOUNDATION, INC.

### PROPOSED BUDGET

2020

- **I.** Economic Considerations and General Ministry Factors The PCA Foundation's (PCAF) primary purpose is to use its assets “.. for the support of the cause of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ, primarily through the Presbyterian Church in America, but also through other groups, societies, organizations, and institutions that minister in Jesus' name to man's spiritual, physical, emotional and intellectual powers." (PCAF Articles of Incorporation)

The purpose of the PCAF is accomplished primarily by providing information, education, and charitable financial services to individuals and families in order to help them carry out their charitable desires and stewardship responsibilities.

The PCAF offers the following charitable financial services: Advise and Consult Funds (donor-advised funds), Charitable Remainder Trusts, Charitable Lead Trusts, Endowments, Designated Funds for Churches, Estate Design, Bequest Processing, and providing educational materials, presentations and information.

The PCAF has experienced significant growth in recent years, which has provided increased revenue streams for operations. As of December 31, 2018, its assets totaled $86.4 million. Compared to the 2013 year-end total assets of $59.8 million, it has increased $26.6 million over the last five years. Improving financial markets over that period and increased awareness of the PCAF's charitable financial services have been significant contributors to the PCAF's growth.

The PCA Foundation's proposed Operating and Capital Budget for 2020 of $1,417,000 represents a $27,000 or 1.9% increase from the 2019 General Assembly approved budget of $1,390,000.

II. Major Changes in Budget There are no major changes in budgeted revenue and expenses included in the proposed 2020 Budget compared to 2019 Budget.

242

<a id="ga47-p245"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=245 printed_page=243 -->

## APPENDIX C

III. Income Streams The PCAF is self-supported. It does not participate in the PCA's Partnership Shares Program, nor does it rely on the financial support of churches to help underwrite its operating expenses.

Approximately 76% of the PCAF's total 2020 budgeted operating revenue is derived from interest/earnings generated by its Advise and Consult Fund, the PCAF Endowment (consistent with prior years) and also several other investments. Trustee/Administrative Fees on Charitable Trusts, Endowments and other accounts are budgeted to provide approximately 20% of the budgeted revenues, and charitable contributions (primarily from a small number of individuals and Board members) account for the remaining 4%. The income streams budgeted for 2020 approximate the same percentages as those budgeted for in recent years.

The sources of revenue and support described above will be attainable and sufficient to provide the 2020 budgeted operating revenues.

IV. Major Ministry Not Implemented in the Past Year There were no new major ministry plans of the PCA Foundation scheduled for implementation during 2018.

- **V.** Notes to Budget “line items”

General Comments The 2020 Operating and Capital Budget of $1,417,000 represents a $27,000 or 1.9% increase compared to the 2019 Budget of $1,390,000.

Notes to Proposed 2020 Budget - (Notes generally relate to the proposed 2020 Budget and address notable variances of the 2020 Budget compared to the 2019 Budget.)

Support & Revenue The 2020 Budget for Support and Revenue is $1,417,000, the amount needed to fund the 2020 Operating and Capital Budget.

Note: The PCA Foundation does not participate in the PCA's Partnership Shares or Ministry Asks programs. It is self-supported.

243

<a id="ga47-p246"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=246 printed_page=244 -->

Undesignated Earnings (line 1) – These payouts are from funds held by the PCA Foundation, mainly from Advise & Consult Funds and the PCAF Endowment, which help underwrite the Foundation's operating expenses. The payout percentages are set annually by the PCA Foundation's Board, and generally are somewhat correlated to the expected investment returns of the accounts. However, during times when the expected investment returns may be lower than the payout amounts needed to fund operations, reserves in these accounts are significantly more than adequate to compensate for the differences. The 2020 Budget of $1,055,000 represents a $10,000, or 1.0% increase from the 2019 Budget amount of $1,045,000.

C & A Support (line 2) – This line was previously used for the total General Assembly mandated support from four Committees and Agencies (Covenant College, Covenant Theological Seminary, Mission to North America and Mission to the World). In 1996, the total amount was $176,000 and was reduced down incrementally to $0 by 2000, the year the Foundation successfully achieved self-supporting status.

Fees (line 3) – 2020 Budgeted fees are administrative fees charged on funds held for long term administration such as Charitable Remainder Trusts, Charitable Lead Trusts, Endowments, and Designated Funds, etc. The 2020 Budget amount of $280,000 is compared to the 2019 Budget amount of $275,000. Current account balances and the anticipation of new accounts in 2020 make achieving the 2020 Budgeted fee income realistic.

Contributions (line 4) – Gifts primarily from a small number of individuals and Board members help underwrite the Foundation's Operating Budget. The contributions budgeted for 2020 are $57,000, compared to $50,000 in the 2019 Budget.

Operations Expenses The 2020 amount budgeted for operating expenses is $1,412,000, compared to $1,357,000 budgeted for 2019, an increase of $55,000 or 4.1%.

Staff Wages & Benefits (lines 6, 7 and 8) – 2020 is budgeted at $967,000, representing an increase of 5.1% or $47,000 from the 2019 Budget amount of $920,000. The increase results primarily from budgeted

244

<a id="ga47-p247"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=247 printed_page=245 -->

## APPENDIX C

salary increases. Wage increases budgeted for 2020 are approximately 3% of estimated 2019 wages.

The 2020 Budget for Staff Wages and Benefits of $967,000 represents an increase of $232,557 over the 2018 Actual of $734,443. However, of this increase, $170,000 is due to the salary and benefits of a Development position which was vacant in 2018. The remainder of the increase of $62,557 over the two-year period is due to wage, payroll tax, health insurance, and retirement plan contribution expense increases, plus increased part-time employee expenses.

All Other Operating Expenses (lines 9-24) – All other operating expenses for the 2020 Budget are $445,000, compared to $437,000 in the 2019 Budget, an increase of $8,000 or 1.8%.

Capital Expenditures Capital Expenditures (line 25) – The 2020 Budget of $30,000 consists of office furniture and fixtures ($8,000) and miscellaneous computer hardware and software to enhance operations and customer service ($22,000).

## APPENDIX C

### PCA RETIREMENT & BENEFITS, INC.

### PROPOSED BUDGET

2020

- **I.** Economic Considerations and General Ministry Factors

- **A.** RBI Vision: That all PCA pastors and their families are wellprepared and cared for in their retirement years. (Note: This vision statement and the mission statement that follows represent the revised vision and mission developed in 2016 as a basis for RBI’$ 5-7 year strategic plan)

- **B.** RBI Mission: To prepare and protect PCA co-laborers in Christ by providing products and guidance in retirement, insurance, relief, and related services. We aim, through trusted relationships with our partners, to enable and encourage them to be more focused on ministry.

- **C.** This budget reflects the costs incurred to administer the trust funds for PCA Retirement & Benefits, Inc. This budget does not reflect the financial activity in those trust funds. (Complete financial activity in the trust funds is provided in the 2018 RBI Annual Report, which includes audited financial statements.)

- **D.** Economic considerations include a CPI of 3.8% (2.5% for the previous year; Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics) during a year of consistently lower unemployment, slowly rising wages, slowly rising interest rates, and stock market (DJIA) decreasing 6% for the year.

II. Major Changes in Budget

- **A.** The 2020 budget reflects a 3.7% increase, or $111,562 all of which is the increase in budgeted expenditures relating to RBI's strategic initiatives. A reduction in planned capital expenditures reduces the overall budget increase to 1.2% compared to the 2018 approved budget (Budget Comparisons). The expense budget changes are spread between line items due to changes in focus from service objectives to strategic initiatives.

- **B.** The total number of staff budgeted for 2020 is 20 FTE compared to 20 FTE in 2019 and 2018, although the composition of the staff is different. The 2018 budget included positions of Development 249

<a id="ga47-p252"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=252 printed_page=250 -->

Officer and Insurance Supervisor. These positions have been eliminated in favor of increased support for Ministry Partner Services and Office Management areas. Salaries are budgeted to increase 3-4% for technical and professional staff to align with market increases and retain top talent.

- **C.** The Retirement portion of Support and Revenue decreased (0.6%), or ($11,948) as a focus on Relief (see E. below) reduces the overall Trustee Fees allocated to Retirement and Insurance. (Budget Comparisons – Line 1).

- **D.** The Insurance portion of Support and Revenue decreased (1.8%), or ($17,839) as a focus on Relief (see E. below) reduces the overall Trustee Fees allocated to Retirement and Insurance. (Budget Comparisons – Line 2).

- **E.** The Relief portion of Support and Revenue shows a 26.2% increase, or $74,784, as a result of a planned update to the 2011 Retirement Readiness Survey and strengthening of Relief staff (Budget Comparisons – Line 3).

- **F.** The Insurance TPA income portion of Support and Revenue reflects fee income collected by RBI for in-house administration of the Insurance plan (Budget Comparisons – Line 4).

- **G.** The 2020 budget reflects $79,500 for capital additions, including office improvements and the replacement of the company car. (Proposed Budget – Line 25)

- **H.** Please note that 2018 actuals are unaudited as of March 15, 2019. The 2018 audit is expected to be complete by April 30, 2019. (Budget Comparisons and Five-Year Comparison).

III. Income Stream The two sources of RBI budgeted revenue are 1) trustee fees charged to the Health and Welfare Benefit Trust, Relief Trust and the Retirement Plan Trust and 2) estimated Insurance In House TPA fees. The trustee fees are set by the General Assembly when it approves our budget.

IV. Major Ministry Not Implemented in the Past Year The budgeted Development Officer was not hired in 2018 as anticipated. Instead, RBI has focused on implementing its 5-7 year

250

<a id="ga47-p253"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=253 printed_page=251 -->

## APPENDIX C

strategic plan. The 2017 and 2018 budgets retained salary and benefits placeholders for the Development Officer. The 2019 budget redirected the funds for the Development Officer to support staff in the client services and office management areas. The 2020 budget will continue to focus on completing RBI's strategic initiatives of: organizational strengthening, data unification and management, enhanced communication, and optimization of products/services.

- **V.** Notes to Budget Line Items

- **A.** An overall net increase of 5.0% in salaries and benefits is assumed for 2020 compared to 2019. Budgeted positions assume a 2.5% cost of living factor and a 2.5% merit factor. The increase is primarily due to the strengthening of skills within the organization and market/merit increases, as compared to a decrease in the 2018 to 2019 salary & benefit budget (see IV. above). (Proposed Budget -Lines 5-8).

- **B.** Occupancy expense for the shared facility is expected to remain at the same rate of $12 per square foot. (Proposed Budget – Line 13).

- **C.** Board meeting expense has increased 27.3% due to the increase in travel and administration costs, as well as number of Advisory Board Members. (Budget Comparisons Statement – Line 7)

- **D.** All fundraising activities relate to the Ministerial Relief program through our development activities, annual Relief Offering, appeals through PCA Foundation and advertising in denominational publications (Proposed Budget – Fundraising Column). The 2020 budget reflects an estimate of 50% of the Relief Director's time spent on fundraising in lieu of a Development Officer. During 2020, the Relief program will, in conjunction with RBI Operations, conduct a Pastoral Resiliency Survey to determine ways RBI can provide services that enable pastors to gain skills to improve their ministries.

- **E.** Our General Assembly line item includes RBI's share of the Nominating Committee expense and any Ad Hoc Committee expense, the cost of convention services, such as booth space and electrical supply, transportation of materials to and from General Assembly, seminars and other education/information activities presented at General Assembly. It also includes RBI's share of denominational legal expense. It does not include travel expense for staff and presenting board members (Five-Year Comparison – Line 10).

## APPENDIX C

### RIDGE HAVEN

Brevard - Cono

### PROPOSED BUDGET

2020

- **I.** Economic Considerations and General Ministry Factors It is hard to put into words the joy granted to us as the Lord continues to bless our ministry. Every year we anticipate this is the year where we will plateau and yet the Lord pours out even more blessings on us. And yes, for our good and to keep us on our knees to trust Him fully, He also allows times of testing. This year has seen some incredible mountain top experiences, but some valleys as well. Still, in all we give Him the glory.

In the valleys we saw the husband of one of our long-term staff members pass away unexpectedly; we got news right before Christmas that a young man who had been a camper and one of our previous Camp Summer Interns, died in an automobile accident; last fall at the height of our fall season, our bookkeeper and another staff member left to open a wonderful coffee shop in Brevard; and seven months after opening Ridge Haven Cono in Iowa, we discovered a major regulatory issue that required repairs to our sewer plant, that delayed our camp ministry expanding into fall and spring retreats this year. Our new capital campaign noted below will address this need.

But through all this, we saw our most successful ministry to date, both in sheer numbers and seeing lives changed and the Kingdom expanded. What an incredible year. For the first time ever, we hosted over 5,000 this summer and over 10,000 for the whole year.

While we started with only a couple weeks of camp at RH Cono last summer, they were fantastic. The incredible indoor gym and activity center are perfect for camp and for cooling off after a morning or afternoon of activities on one of the two full-size soccer fields. Of course, we had our own "Hillbilly pool" made from hundreds of hay bales, and atop “Mount Cono” a 100’ by 100’ water slide that was quite the hit.

At RH Brevard we were excited to host many RUF and other campus ministries. A highlight of the fall was hosting the Western Carolina Presbytery Women's retreat with speaker Nancy Guthrie, for over 300 ladies. We also had well over 100 different church groups and over 30 college ministry groups throughout the year. Our new Spartan race 255

<a id="ga47-p258"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=258 printed_page=256 -->

course has been a popular addition to our many activities, and as always our inner city ministry week is one of the best activities of the whole year. What a blessing to serve our denomination in this way. Thank you for the opportunity.

II. Major Changes in Budget Our Board just approved a $5,000,000 capital campaign with the goal of building a multipurpose meeting and activity center, additional housing in Brevard, a small chapel, and acquiring essential equipment around campus. We are also thrilled to announce that TE Archie Moore will move from part time to full-time Campus Pastor early in 2020. The campaign will also cover our acquisition debt for RH Cono and add sprinklers to the buildings to allow full year use of our facilities. An indoor activity pool will complete a full complement of amenities to serve our camps and conferences, and to enhance our ministries to the local community.

III. Support/Revenue Streams Ridge Haven receives support/revenue from the following sources:

1. Camp, Conference, and Retreat Fees (includes food service and bookstore revenue)

2. Facility and farmland (Cono) rental.

3. Contributions (includes partnership shares and direct contributions)

4. Minor sources of revenue, which include resident fees (water/sewer fees, road assessments, etc.), and interest-bearing bank accounts.

IV. Major Ministry Not Implemented in the Past Year One of the most disappointing things we do is turn away groups interested in booking a retreat for over 350 guests in late fall, winter and early spring as we do not have an indoor place for meetings. Twice just this year we have had to do so. By God's grace giving us our new Jolly Dining Hall and 13 new cabins, we can sleep and feed well over 700, but there is nowhere for them to meet except at our outdoor Barnes Center. As noted above, we are currently pursuing funding for a new indoor multipurpose meeting and activity center that can accommodate large groups for meetings and indoor activities.

- **V.** 2020 Budget Line Items Notes All notes refer both to the Proposed Budget and the Budget Comparison Inserts

## APPENDIX C

Line 1, 2, & 3, Camps, Conferences, Retreats – In 2018, we made significant changes to what is classified under these headings. For example, Camp Income now represents camps where we supply the counselors. Retreats now represent church groups, etc. that supply their own counselors. Conferences are now strictly events where we supply the entire program and speaker etc. Historical comparisons are accordingly difficult.

Line 4, Property – This line item includes revenue from lot maintenance  
fees, water hookups, water usage fees, and road maintenance fees from  
18 lots which are contiguous to our main campus. The amount budgeted  
each year reflects the predictable aspects of this revenue, i.e. the principal  
and interest being paid on lot leases being bought over time, the annually  
collected lot lease maintenance fees, water usage fees, and a portion of  
the road maintenance fees.

Line 8, Miscellaneous – Includes refund of state sales tax, amortization of lot leases, Right-of-Way land sales, staff rentals, and interest revenue.

Line 10, Payroll and Benefits – Includes payroll and benefits for 19 yearround employees, plus part-time counselors, and summer/weekend staff both for Ridge Haven Brevard, and Ridge Haven Cono. Camp and conference leaders, speakers, and musicians' honorariums and travel expenses are included in this category, as well as payroll taxes and workers' compensation insurance.

Line 12, Office and Administrative – Includes major expense items, including commercial insurance, telephone fees, office and housekeeping supplies, loan interest and bank fees, and audit and legal fees.

Line 14, Facilities – Includes repairs, deferred maintenance, real estate taxes, and refuse expenses.

Line 16, Ministry – Includes camp and retreat supplies, camp registration software fees, and travel and other expenses associated with our camp for inner-city kids.

Line 17, Recruiting – Includes all printing costs, promotional ads and media productions, and recruitment initiatives and trips.

Line 23, Capital Campaign – Start-up and production costs.

Line 24, Cono Expenses – In the 2018 Budget, we did not categorize items. Now, after the first year, we have a better indication of what and where our expenses are allocated.

### 2020 PARTNERSHIP SHARES STATEMENT

### FOR THE PCA GENERAL ASSEMBLY MINISTRIES

### PREFACE

The working definition under which the 2020 Partnership Share Budgets have been calculated is as follows. As a general statement, “Partnership Shares” describes the amount of money needed to cover the anticipated total expenses of a ministry minus earned income and minus funds designated to specific individuals who are missionaries, church planters, campus ministers, and staff (unless the ministry also guarantees the full compensation of the employee), as well as specific capital funds or similar designated monies. This portion of the approved expense budget is dependent on contributions from the PCA churches and individuals. In every case the “Partnership Share” is permitted to be at least the General Administrative and Overhead portion of the particular ministry’s total budget. Two important numbers for each participating ministry are provided by the Partnership Share and Ministry Ask calculations. First, the numbers located in the column labeled “Per Capita Calculation" are obtained by a per capita giving formula, which divides the Partnership Share Fund amount for each General Assembly Ministry by the total number of communicant members last reported to and accumulated by the Office of the Stated Clerk. A second set of numbers under the column labeled “Ministry Ask” is provided for churches. The “Ministry Ask" is the amount of money each Committee or Agency is asking the churches of the PCA to give if the church would like to give to PCA Ministries on a “per member” basis. The amount listed in this column is generally an estimate of what each Committee and Agency needs to receive from each donor church per member in order for the Committee or Agency to raise their full budget approved by the PCA General Assembly. These two numbers provide churches and individuals with important factors as they seek to decide how to give to the PCA General Assembly Committees and Agencies. All PCA Ministries struggle to raise Partnership Share funds, and none of the PCA ministries would be sustained without generous donors who give far beyond the Partnership Share. Please assist as generously as you are able. In short, the Partnership Shares calculation is based on the inaccurate assumption that all churches have the same giving capacity per member and that all churches will give to all Committees and Agencies. The Ministry Ask is a more realistic figure. 262

## APPENDIX D

### REPORT OF

### THE COMMITTEE ON DISCIPLESHIP MINISTRIES

### TO THE FORTY-SEVENTH GENERAL ASSEMBLY

### OF THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA

“... but just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak, not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts. So, being affectionately desirous of you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become dear to us." (1 Thessalonians 2:4, 8 ESV)

Biblical discipleship is a presentation of the God-given truth of salvation that flows from a God-given affection for those he has placed in your life. Discipleship presents the life-transforming truth of God's Word in the context of relationships. The Committee on Discipleship Ministries (CDM) exists to strengthen the local church by connecting leaders to the people and resources they need to make disciples in the ministry to children, youth, and adults. We pursue that mission through connection: connecting people to people, and people to resources. Churches in the PCA share the same commitment to Scripture and the Westminster Standards, but we do ministry in very different contexts. The various expressions of gospel ministry can bring blessing. Together, we are stronger.

Connecting People to People CDM staff members and consultants nurture relational connections primarily through individual contact, local training events, and regional conferences. Ministry coordinators make daily contact with local church leaders through e-mail, telephone calls, and face-to-face conversations. The questions span the spectrum of discipleship ministry from the youngest children to the oldest child of God. Questions range from “Can you help with...?" to “Who can I talk to about...?" to “Where can I go for...?" The contact information for them is on the CDM website (pcacdm.org/about-cdm/cdm-staff).

Local training events include seminars on women's ministry, children's ministry, parenting, and leadership development. The training is conducted by CDM staff members or members of our ministry teams for children,

264

<a id="ga47-p267"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=267 printed_page=265 -->

## APPENDIX D

youth, or women. If you would like to schedule an event, contact the CDM office through our website at pcacdm.org/contact-cdm. In 2018, CDM worked with local churches to host a series of regional training opportunities. ONE conferences for women were held in Jackson, MS, Annapolis, MD, Chattanooga, TN, and St. Louis, MO. Plenary sessions centered on the theme of unity in the Body of Christ according to Jesus' prayer in John 17. Workshop sessions were tailored to contextualize biblical truth according to the needs and issues facing the region of the host church.

Due to the generosity of a donor, CDM continued to partner with host churches to offer five Established conferences for those who serve in children's ministry. Events were held in Naples, FL, Rochester, MN, Olathe, KS, Boston, MA, and Indianapolis, IN. The theme centered on Psalm 78 and the ways covenant theology shapes ministry to children. CDM staff members worked with the host churches to design sessions to meet the needs of the region.

Financial Review The ministry of CDM is funded through a combination of revenue sources:

1. giving from churches, 2) giving from individuals, 3) revenue from the sale of resources, and 4) revenue from conference fees. CDM ended 2018 with a nominal operating deficit of -$10,992 (or 0.7%). Ironically, the loss was primarily attributable to the abrupt downturn in the stock market in the fourth quarter of 2018, which caused CDM's investments to decline -$20,000. Thankfully, the market rebounded in January 2019 and approximately half of the year-end loss was quickly recovered. CDM continues to have an operating reserve greater than the goal of six months of contribution income. CDM's financial success in 2018 was primarily due to surpluses realized through fees for the regional conferences and the large donation given to underwrite the Established Conferences. This is the third straight year that God has provided for CDM through conference proceeds and/or extraordinarily large gifts from individuals.

Since the beginning of the denomination, CDM's primary source of income has been support from PCA congregations (BCO 14-1). However, only 29% of PCA particular churches contribute financially to the ministry of CDM. This reality is discouraging to the members of the staff and permanent committee, as CDM has been hindered in providing training and resources for ministry to youth, men, and older adults. Together, we could be stronger.

8. That the General Assembly re-elect TE Stephen Estock to serve as the Coordinator for the Committee on Discipleship Ministries (CDM).

9. That Overture 11 from Fellowship Presbytery “Commend and Distribute RPCNA's ‘Contemporary Perspectives on Sexual Orientation: A Theological and Pastoral Analysis" be answered in the negative. Grounds:

- **(1)** The report mentioned in the Overture was published by Crown & Covenant Publications in 2012 under the title The Gospel & Sexual Orientation (Michael Lefebvre, Editor). Given that the material is under copyright with Crown & Covenant Publications and The Synod of the Reformed Presbyterian Church of North America (RPCNA), the overture is improper and out of order in that it asks the GA and CDM to do something that would require legal permission which they do not currently have (RRO 39, 11th ed., p. 343).

- **(2)** The Gospel & Sexual Orientation is in print and available from CDM through the PCA Bookstore (pcabookstore.com, item #11555). It is also available publicly at the URL indicated in the Overture.

- **(3)** The overture directs the production of curriculum without any consideration for the proper funding to complete the project (see also point 1 above).

10. That Overture 24 from Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery "Add Constitutional Precedence Statement to Policy Manuals" be answered by reference to the recommendation from the Administrative Committee regarding Overture 24.

11. That Overture 25 from Suncoast Florida Presbytery “Support Christian Education” be answered in the negative. Grounds:

- **(1)** The overture is unnecessary. Scripture clearly teaches that parents have the responsibility for the education of covenant children (Deut. 6, Eph. 6). Church Sessions have the power "to determine the best measures for promoting the spiritual interests of the church and congregation" (BCO 12-5.e). The General Assembly does not need to affirm what Scripture clearly teaches and the Constitution already provides.

- **(2)** The particular method(s) used by parents to fulfill their scriptural responsibility is a matter of conscience, guided by the Holy Spirit and informed by the Word of God and the pastoral counsel of elders in the local church. It is inappropriate for the General Assembly to direct parents (explicitly or implicitly) to a particular method. The 270

<a id="ga47-p273"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=273 printed_page=271 -->

## APPENDIX D

overture may (unintentionally) bind the conscience of a parent attempting to fulfill his/her scriptural responsibility.

- **(3)** The overture is vague in some of its stipulations. For example, the overture fails to define “a wholly Christian education." Likewise, “financial, spiritual, and instructional assistance” that is “helpful” is vague. The Constitution already stipulates the office of deacon is provided for “helping one another in time of need" (BCO 9-1) and "it is the duty of the deacons to minister to those who are in need" (BCO 9-2).

12. That the General Assembly approve the 2020 CDM budget as presented by the Administrative Committee.

### REPORT FROM THE PUBLISHING MINISTRY OF

### GREAT COMMISSION PUBLICATIONS (GCP)

Great Commission Publications (GCP) is the official publishing ministry of the PCA and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church (OPC). This joint publishing ministry was established by the respective General Assemblies in 1975. GCP publishes high-quality Reformed and covenantal curriculum for all ages. This full-orbed system of curriculum is based solely upon the Bible as the Word of God and conforms to the Westminster Standards.

GCP is governed by a twelve-member board of trustees, all teaching or ruling elders. Six are elected by the PCA CDM and six by the OPC Committee on Christian Education (CCE). Additionally, the PCA CDM Coordinator and the OPC CCE General Secretary serve as ex-officio, non-voting trustees. Currently the GCP Executive Director and the Director of Publishing are PCA teaching elders. The GCP Director of Business Operations is a PCA ruling elder. The President of the board of trustees for 2019 is OPC teaching elder Dr. Alan Strange.

Our newest curriculum is "G2R—God's Promises," written to teach covenant theology to grades 7-9. (G2R is an abbreviation for “Genesis to Revelation.") “G2R—God's Promises” completes the G2R curriculum, which begins with Bible surveys of the Old Testament and the New Testament. This survey of all the Old and New Testament books helps students integrate the "stories" of the Bible they have heard into a comprehensive understanding of God's single story of his redemptive plan throughout Scripture. Both departments allow churches great flexibility in how to group grades 7-9. Check out www.gcp.org to see how to use these studies. Upon completion of the G2R curriculum, students should be well grounded not only in the entire Bible, but with the essence of covenant theology.

GCP also publishes Trinity Hymnal, a resource that enriches worship with its collection of over 700 hymns. It includes the Westminster Confession of Faith, as well the Creeds. Orchestrations are available for most of the hymns.

Show Me Jesus (Toddler through fourth grade) is the core upon which all the rest of GCP's curriculum is built. Further, Kids’ Quest is a club program that is a catechetical curriculum (First Catechism) suited for use in many 272

<a id="ga47-p275"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=275 printed_page=273 -->

## APPENDIX D

settings of church life. GCP also has a pocket edition of First Catechism for use by all ages, as well as digital editions of First Catechism and the Shorter Catechism. G2R follows Show Me Jesus, and is followed by So What? for high school students

So What? Bible studies for youth continue to grow in popularity. There are ten studies available in a modular format, which makes them flexible for youth groups, small group Bible studies, homeschools, and Christian day schools. Visit the So What? website at www.sowhatstudies.org for samples, video previews, and more.

GCP publishes a child's curriculum based on The Pilgrim's Progress. It features a new child's edition of the book, a dramatic reading, and a selection of original songs, as well as lessons. For sample lessons, please visit www.childrenspilgrimsprogress.org.

Please visit our website at www.gcp.org to order or call 800-695-3387 to speak to a curriculum specialist.

God's Word for God's World: Building on Biblical Foundations for Training Impactful Gospel Leaders

Executive Summary Last year, we reported on several important changes as the Seminary launched new degrees and degree formats. We introduced a new church planting track and 30 percent church-match scholarships to better serve the needs of the PCA. We grew our online offerings to meet the changing educational needs of today's world. Promotions to positions of greater responsibility for several longserving, faithful members of our deeply biblical and Reformed faculty, with key additions to our adjunct faculty. being drafted and submitted to GA, and the impression it gives of a desire on our part to no longer be under the oversight of the PCA is incorrect and unfounded.

God's Word for God's World: Building on Biblical Foundations for Training Impactful Gospel Leaders

The purpose of Covenant Theological Seminary is to glorify the triune God by training his servants to walk in God’s grace, minister God’s Word, and equip God's people—all for God's mission. Last year, we reported on several important changes in how we carry out that purpose: we launched some new degrees, restructured others, introduced a new church planting track and 30 percent church-match scholarships, and grew our online offerings to meet the changing educational needs of today's world. We are thankful for the way the Lord has blessed these efforts so that the church can receive more of the biblically trained and qualified leaders it needs and deserves. This year, we built on these initiatives in several significant ways.

New Degrees, New Flexible Ways to Learn To better meet the growing need in the church for training that is biblical, accessible, and flexible, Covenant Seminary last fall introduced two new degree programs. These are designed to help students get the training they need for their unique ministry or life callings without necessarily relocating to St. Louis. The degrees also enabled us to offer a new hybrid-format Master of Divinity in addition to our traditional residential MDiv program.

The Master of Arts (Biblical and Theological Studies) (MABTS)—available both on-campus and fully online—is ideal for ministry leaders who do not have the opportunity to complete a degree in residence or who simply desire more robust biblical training than most online programs provide. It is also a good option for those who feel called to teach in the church or academy. The degree also enables students to complete two-thirds of an MDiv online. The MABTS:

281

<a id="ga47-p284"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=284 printed_page=282 -->

O Requires study of at least one biblical language (Greek or Hebrew)—though students may take both if they desire and can be done completely online. O Offers an optional thesis for those who wish to prepare for a PhD. O Allows for easy transfer into the MDiv program for those who wish to complete a final third of the MDiv through week-long visits to campus for intensive courses. O Requires 66 total credit hours and may be completed in 2 – 4 years.

The Master of Arts in Ministry (MAM)—available on campus or in a hybrid online/on-campus format—is perfect for people who sense a call to ministry but need a season of more immersive preparation. It is also a good choice for busy ministry leaders unable to relocate to complete their training but who desire a biblical and practical degree to better equip them for the work to which the Lord has already called them. The MAM:

O Offers great flexibility for students to tailor their degree to their particular needs. All MAM students take substantial core courses providing foundations in Bible and theology, with a wide range of electives to spread across classes in biblical studies and applied theology. O Provides students the opportunity to focus electives into a concentration area to better equip them for their unique ministry contexts or goals. The MAM General Track may be done in a hybrid (online/on-campus) format with as few as 4 one-week visits to campus for intensive courses. In addition, the program offers five potential concentration tracks:

Biblical Studies and Christian Ministry — Ideal for the ministry leader who wants to handle and communicate God's Word and care for his people. This track may be done in a hybrid format with as few as 5 one-week visits to campus for intensive courses. City Ministry — Ideal for those called to minister in an urban context, whether in the church or outside of it. This track tracks require several semester-long on-campus courses.

<a id="ga47-p285"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=285 printed_page=283 -->

## APPENDIX F

Counseling Ministries — Ideal for those not seeking professional licensure but who are involved in counseling ministries such as recovery groups, diaconal ministry, mercy ministry, etc. This track may be done in a hybrid format with as few as 5 oneweek visits to campus for intensive courses. Cultural Apologetics and Communication 一 Ideal for those who want to be equipped to address the issues of our day in a biblical, thoughtful and winsome way. This track tracks require several semester-long on-campus courses. Educational Ministries — Ideal for ministry directors (women, youth, children's, etc.) or anyone called to make disciples in a non-ordained setting. This track tracks require several semester-long oncampus courses.

O Requires 200 hours of supervised field education work in an approved ministry setting. O Requires 54 total credit hours and may be completed in 2 – 4 years.

The Master of Divinity (MDiv) can now also be completed in a hybrid format. Two-thirds of the degree may be completed online with the rest being completed in as few as 6 one-week trips to campus. While we remain as devoted as ever to residential-based mentored ministry training, our students now have even greater flexibility in how they choose to study.

The MABTS online and MAM hybrid options also have built-in community learning components so that students not physically on campus can still experience the benefits of learning and growing together with their peers and professors.

The MDiv Church Planting Track: Pathway to Church Planting The Seminary last year inaugurated a Church Planting Track for the MDiv program. The track is designed to meet the increasing need for church planters in the PCA. Students interested in and gifted for church planting now have a way to concentrate their studies for deeper preparedness upon graduation. Students may pursue the Church Planting Track through

283

<a id="ga47-p286"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=286 printed_page=284 -->

on-campus residential study or through the hybrid MDiv format, using a combination of online and on-campus intensive (week-long or weekend) courses to complete the degree. The track offers:

Classes focused specifically on church planting and related issues. Multiple professional assessments of gifting and readiness to be a church planter. Mentored oversight and regular evaluation of developing church planters. Church planting internship and apprenticeship opportunities that fulfill Field Education and Presbytery internship requirements. Training in fundraising and related issues. A limited number of Church Planting Scholarships each year for qualified students.

New DMin Cohort on Cultural Apologetics and Communication Our Doctor of Ministry team this spring launched a new Cultural Apologetics and Communication cohort, led by Professors Mark Ryan, Tasha Chapman, and Zack Eswine. The cohort draws on the ethos and expertise of the Francis A. Schaeffer Institute to help pastors and others in ministry learn how to engage people effectively and winsomely with the gospel in a world where “truth" changes almost daily. Instructors include Covenant Seminary's own Prof. Jerram Barrs, Dr. Michael Williams, and Dr. Michael Goheen, as well as guest lecturers such as Grace DC Institute for Cross-Cultural Mission's Executive Director Rev. Dr. Irwyn Ince. The current iteration of the cohort begins meeting this June and is closed for new registrations, but our Admissions team is eager to talk with interested parties about future editions.

30% Church-Match Scholarships for All Degree Programs Churches now have a powerful way to partner with Covenant Seminary in helping potential pastors and church leaders get the training they need to minister effectively. The Seminary now offers a Church-Match Scholarship program for students receiving seminary funding from their churches. The scholarship matches up to 30% of a student's tuition cost, totaling a 60% tuition reduction for qualifying students.

The Church-Match Scholarship is available for students in all of Covenant's degree programs and all learning formats (except for those through the Missional Training Center-Phoenix), which includes those studying full-time, part-time, on campus, online, or through one of our new hybrid-format options. 284

## APPENDIX F

Along with the new scholarship, we have also retooled our scholarship structure in general to offer even more benefits to students in our online and hybrid degree programs, including higher scholarship amounts and longer-term scholarship availability.

All hybrid-format Master of Divinity (MDiv) scholarships will last for six years, allowing students in that program to take courses part-time. Online Master of Arts (Biblical and Theological Studies) (MABTS) students are eligible for scholarships lasting for fiveyear terms. Online Master of Arts (Theological Studies) (MATS) and hybridformat Master of Arts in Ministry (MAM) scholarships are available for four-year terms.

Covenant + NEXT Partnership = Expanded Training for Next- Generation Ministry In 2018 we formed a partnership with NEXT (formerly Global Youth and Family Ministries) that will give Covenant's ministry-leaders-intraining greater access to the knowledge and expertise of NEXT's experienced staff and provide NEXT with a new hub of operations for its global ministry. The distinctive partnership enables both organizations to better provide strategic training for shaping a new generation of local church leaders with a global mindset. Founded by Covenant Seminary alumnus Dr. Eric Larsen, NEXT (a ministry of MTW) is focused on equipping missionaries, national leaders, and indigenous churches around the world to reach the youth in their communities with the gospel. Larsen holds a doctorate in youth, family, and culture, and is the author of MissionNext: How the Church Can Reach a Global Generation (Doulos Resources, 2017). He has taught courses on next-generation ministry at Covenant and other Christian institutions for many years. Under the partnership, he continues to teach key courses in Covenant's youth ministry curriculum and consults regularly with Seminary faculty, staff, and alumni on best practices for reaching and equipping emerging generations for ministry.

Edinburgh Summer School: Transformative Learning in a Unique Setting Covenant Seminary continues to partner with the Chalmers Institute in St. Andrews to deliver a week-long summer school combining the best theological resources with application to the church's discipleship and mission. Previously held in Cambridge, England, this year's edition of our summer school program offers a unique opportunity for pastors, scholars,

285

<a id="ga47-p288"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=288 printed_page=286 -->

and others to deepen their theological learning and insight while studying in the beautiful location of Edinburgh, Scotland. Students will gain a deeper understanding of who God is, what he has called us to do as his people, how we can understand the Bible, and how to engage our neighbors with his lifegiving message. The July 2019 edition features Dr. Jack Collins teaching a track on the Psalms and Wisdom Literature, while Prof. Jerram Barrs and Dr. Mark Stirling (director of the Chalmers Institute) lead a track on Engaging Contemporary Challenges to Christianity. You can find more at www.covenantseminary.edu/ academics/edinburgh/.

New Faculty Blog: Orthodoxy and Orthopraxy How we understand theology affects how we live that theology out. That's why Covenant Seminary's faculty came together to produce a new theology blog on our website called Orthodoxy and Orthopraxy. In regular posts, faculty address thoughtfully and biblically a variety of theological topics and issues of our day, and provide insight for Christian living and compassionate gospel witness in our confused and hurting world. Check out Orthodoxy and Orthopraxy on our homepage at www.covenantseminary.edu.

Same Mission, New Logo In 2018, we rolled out a new version of the Covenant Seminary logo with updates to our website and print publications to reflect the new look and style. This was the first complete logo and branding redesign for the institution in nearly 20 years. The goal for the redesign was to build on the historical imagery of earlier versions of our logo while crafting a look that feels more contemporary. While our mission and theological commitments remain the same as always, we wanted our new logo to better reflect both our long heritage of biblical, Reformed theological education and our continuing dedication to preparing church leaders and Kingdom workers who can communicate God's gospel of grace and truth in powerful and relevant ways in today's world.

Celebrating 30 Years of the Francis Schaeffer Institute This year marks three decades since the Francis Schaeffer Institute (FSI) was founded at Covenant Seminary to extend and embody the legacy of renowned pastor and apologist Francis A. Schaeffer. Established in 1989 by Professor Jerram Barrs, a student and coworker of Dr. Schaeffer and longtime director of the English branch of L'Abri Fellowship, FSI has had a profound impact on the formation of countless church and Kingdom leaders.

Covenant Seminary Preaching Lectures: Scriptural Wisdom for Communicating God's Word Preaching is key to the mission and ministry of the church. Preparing good preachers is one of our main goals at Covenant Seminary. In addition to our Christ-centered, grace-focused, and apologetically oriented preaching curriculum, the Seminary each year invites recognized leaders in the field of homiletics to speak on topics relevant to communicating God's Word effectively in today's world. The 2018 Preaching Lectures featured our own Dr. Zack Eswine, director of homiletics and scholar-in-residence with FSI, speaking on the theme Sage Voice: How the Wisdom Literature Equips Us to Communicate Jesus in the 21st Century. Dr. Eswine presented insights from the biblical Wisdom Literature to help preachers find points of contact with the swirling cultural voices of our generation and address wisely the concerns and questions that raise doubts and suspicions about the gospel. Audio from the Preaching Lectures is available at www.covenantseminary.edu/resources.

The Austin Harrington Counseling Lectures: The Science of Virtue The Austin Harrington Counseling Lectures, sponsored by the Seminary's Counseling Department, each year brings in notable authorities in the field of Christian counseling to provide additional instruction and resources for those training to serve God's people as pastors and counselors. For 2019, the theme was The Science of Virtue: Positive Psychology, Counseling, and the Church. Featured speaker Dr. Mark McMinn, professor of psychology and faith integration with George Fox University's Graduate Department of Clinical Psychology, showed how virtues that Christians have considered essential for centuries are now being explored in social science laboratories all over the world—though the faith element inherent in those virtues often is not. Dr. McMinn urged that dialogue between psychology, theology, and counseling is essential to building bridges that benefit both the church and science. Audio is online at www.covenantseminary.edu/resources. The Professional Counselor Training Series: Continuing Education for Practicing Counselors The inaugural Professional Counselor Training Series to provide professional counselors licensed in the state of Missouri with quality continuing education units in which Covenant counseling faculty help 288

“Trauma + Sexuality” “Trauma + Lament” “Trauma + Attachment"

Faculty / Staff Updates The Lord's greatest gift to Covenant Seminary is the people who serve here as faculty, staff, or trustees. We have been particularly blessed in this regard, as the following updates on our personnel and their Kingdom service indicate.

Prof. Suzanne Bates, who has taught as adjunct professor of applied Theology (counseling) since 2010, was recently promoted to assistant professor of counseling. Prof. Bates holds an MAC from Covenant Seminary and is currently pursuing a PhD in counseling education at the University of Missouri-St. Louis. She is a licensed professional counselor who serves as a staff counselor and ministry director at New City Fellowship (PCA) in St. Louis, and has been a case worker in the St. Louis County Department of Justice Services and a counselor for the Community Action Agency of St. Louis, where she worked with the prison population. She also serves as the Seminary's associate dean of students for women and is a regular speaker at conferences and women's retreats. Dr. Tasha Chapman, formerly director of educational studies and adjunct associate professor of educational ministries, was promoted to professor of educational ministries. She holds a PhD in educational studies from Trinity Evangelical Divinity School and 293

<a id="ga47-p296"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=296 printed_page=294 -->

has taught at Covenant in various capacities since 2004. Her current consulting and research focuses on leadership and self-stewardship in ministry, cross-cultural learning, and instructional and curriculum design. She is the co-author (with Bob Burns and Donald Guthrie) of Resilient Ministry: What Pastors Told Us About Surviving and Thriving (IVP, 2013) and its follow-up The Politics of Ministry: Navigating Power Dynamics and Negotiating Interests (IVP, 2018). Prior to Covenant, Dr. Chapman worked in campus ministry and as director of women's ministry in a local church. Dr. Zack Eswine, director of homiletics and adjunct professor of homiletics, and his wife, Jessica Eswine, a trained lawyer and Christian apologist, joined the staff of the Francis Schaeffer Institute (FSI). Dr. Eswine will now also serve as scholar-inresidence for FSI. Mrs. Eswine will serve as visiting instructor of integrated apologetics. Dr. Eswine will join FSI Director Prof. Mark Ryan and FSI founder and Senior Scholar-in-Residence Prof. Jerram Barrs in offering new MA and DMin degree tracks in communication and cultural apologetics. He will continue to teach for and direct the homiletics program and to serve as pastor at Riverside Community Church in Webster Groves, Missouri, where he has been since 2008. Mrs. Eswine will also teach apologetics courses for FSI. Dr. Michael W. Goheen, director of theological education for the Missional Training Center (MTC)-Phoenix, joined the faculty of Covenant Theological Seminary as professor of missional theology in July 2018. In addition to his ongoing directorial and teaching work with MTC—which became an extension site of Covenant in 2017— Dr. Goheen will teach occasional courses on mission-related topics at the Seminary. A pastor, church planter, scholar, and recognized authority on mission in today's world, Dr. Goheen's work with MTC provides deeper theological training in a non-traditional, missionoriented educational setting for those currently serving in ministry. He also serves as scholar-in-residence for Surge Network, a Phoenix-based church-leadership training network. Dr. Goheen has authored, co-authored, or edited several books, including A Light to the Nations (IVP, 2014), Introducing Christian Mission Today (Baker, 2011), and The Church and Its Vocation: (Baker, 2018). Prof. Aaron Goldstein was recently appointed associate director of online learning and adjunct professor of Old Testament. responsibilities as the Seminary's interim assistant director of online learning before being named associate director of online learning and adjunct professor of Old Testament later that year. Dr. Joel Hathaway, director of alumni and career services, took on the additional and complementary role of director of the Doctor of Ministry program in 2018. Financial Growth and Stability In line with our audited financials, the Seminary finished last year with $9,815,147 in total revenues, which included $2,762,836 from net tuition; $6,217,697 in total giving; and $841,482 from auxiliary enterprises revenue. Additionally, the endowment gained $1,321,148 in investment income from endowment assets, and $1,059,211 was released from the endowment into the operating revenues. Gifts received were at a six-year high due in large part to the success of the current capital campaign. Rationale: Covenant Seminary was shocked to hear of this overture as we were in no way consulted on this overture. Covenant Seminary does not and never has desired to be released from PCA oversight but rather delights in and values deeply the oversight provided through the General Assembly-elected ruling and teaching elders. ## APPENDIX F

Covenant Seminary believes that authoritative oversight of the Seminary by ordained elders is particularly important and vital for the task of training men who will be ordained pastors in the PCA. Then Covenant Seminary President Dr. Will Barker stated at the 10th General Assembly that “theological education should be under the denomination's-auspices and responsible to the church. Our history has been blessed through this orientation to the work of the church." We continue to believe this, desire this, and are blessed by this official and formal relationship. Between 1981 and 1982 all 25 PCA presbyteries voted to receive the RPCES into the PCA with the understanding that Covenant College and Covenant Seminary would be received into the PCA and have their own Committees of Commissioners at General Assembly. Elders who serve on the Board of Trustees are recommended by presbyteries to the GA Nominating Committee, which then recommends an annual slate of board nominees who are voted on by the General Assembly. The members of the Board of Trustees elect the president, approve faculty members, adopt the budget, and oversee the Seminary's doctrinal and educational work of training, equipping, and sending graduates into the church. Elected members of the Board of Trustees annually reaffirm by signature their commitment to the system of doctrine taught in the Westminster Standards. The approval of the General Assembly Theological Examining Committee is necessary for each newly elected president to take up the office of president. The Presbytery-elected Committee of Commissioners reviews the work of the Seminary each year and brings recommendations to the General Assembly. The above-named oversight and accountability provide mutual benefit to the PCA and to Covenant Seminary by maintaining our shared conviction to be faithfully committed to the inerrancy of the Bible, the historic Reformed faith, and the great commission. It is our deep desire and delight to continue to serve as the denominational seminary of the PCA as we strive to "glorify the triune God by training his servants to walk in God's grace, minister God's Word, and equip God's people—all for God's mission."

## APPENDIX G

### REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON

### MISSION TO NORTH AMERICA

### TO THE FORTY-SEVENTH GENERAL ASSEMBLY

### OFTHE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA

...Standing firm in one spirit, with one mind striving side by side for the faith of the gospel... Philippians 1:27

MNA Calling and Vision: The calling of Mission to North America (MNA) is to serve Presbyterian Church in America (PCA) members, congregations, presbyteries, networks, and the Assembly as a whole as a catalyst for the progress of the gospel, down deeper into our lives and out wider into the communities of the United States and Canada. Catalysts in nature enable chemical reactions to take place more efficiently and bountifully; MNA seeks to be a catalyst for the vibrancy and extension of the church throughout North America. Therefore, MNA exists to celebrate and share the gospel of Jesus Christ in the United States and Canada by coming alongside the local and regional church in church planting, church renewal, and missional partnerships.

MNA Thanksgivings: Please join with me in rejoicing in God's gracious provision for MNA, as we not only saw major funding pass through our stewardship for designated gifts to support church planting, disaster response, chaplain ministries, and other efforts in mission and renewal, but we also finished 2018 with a surplus in MNA's Ministry Support Fund. The MSF has been renamed the MNA General Fund, because it supports and undergirds all MNA does in the field. Developing sufficient income for the General Fund, most of which is provided through PCA church giving in response to the Askings, continues to be one of our greatest challenges. We praise God for his provision of sufficient support again in 2018. Thanks be to God!

MNA Next Steps in Church Planting: With expectation of Christ's kingdom coming in greater fullness among us by the advance of his gospel in depth and breadth throughout North America, MNA is taking a major new step in serving churches, networks, and presbyteries as we strive together side by side for the progress of the gospel through church planting. 300

<a id="ga47-p303"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=303 printed_page=301 -->

## APPENDIX G

Experience demonstrates that church planting expands and flourishes when a church planting “ecosystem” (When we say ecosystem, think in terms of a healthy, thriving lake, farm, forest, or ocean bay.) is in place and thriving in these seven phases: Developing and recruiting church planters and church planting teams (Develop and Recruit) Assessing church planter candidates and their spouses (Assess) Training and assisting church planters in their fundraising (Fundraise) Seeking God's guidance in placing the church planter (Placement) Providing church planter training (Train) Supporting and encouraging the church planter through coaching and mentoring (Coach and Mentor) Celebration and Renewal, reflecting on God's great work thus far and looking to him for greater works in the future. (Celebrate and Renew)

In the early days of the PCA, MNA focused primarily on welcoming churches transferring into the PCA from other denominations. In its next generation, MNA assumed direct responsibility for providing in a centralized fashion the services required for the seven phases of church planting ecosystems. In recent years, MNA has moved steadily toward a resourcing and training role as churches and presbyteries assume a growing ownership and have achieved ever-greater skills in developing local and regional ecosystems for church planting. Thus, MNA serves as catalyst for church planting.

God has blessed the PCA with a strong sense of calling to church planting. 2018 saw God's blessing in sending 50 church planters to the field to begin a new mission church, continuing since 2005 an average of one PCA church planter being placed on the field each week across North America. (See Attachment 1 for the list of the church planters placed in 2018.) While this is a good number for a denomination the size of the PCA, we trust God for more. MNA is moving toward an even greater focus on serving churches, presbyteries, and networks in their development of church planting ecosystems. As a next step, MNA will begin highlighting the seven phases above by providing a growing number of events and identified resource people and organizations to provide growing services in each of the seven phases. In short, if we are to see church planting multiply, it is time for us to pursue new and best pathways for multiplication, so that local and regional systems of church planting begin to reproduce radically. 301

<a id="ga47-p304"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=304 printed_page=302 -->

As we make these changes, MNA church planting services will no longer be coordinated by just one staff member and his assistant. Church Planting Coordinator Ted Powers and Church Planting Assistant Ann Powers have stepped away from their MNA roles after 17 and 21 years, respectively, of faithful service. This change brings sadness in what it means personally for the many who have worked alongside Ted and Ann, and at the same time it comes with great thanksgiving for the many ways in which God has led and worked through them. In this new approach, our goal is to multiply the services they performed while serving with MNA. Our prayers are with them as we all continue in the journey of following Jesus and serving in his kingdom. As one of the core services that MNA provides, we expect to continue conducting centralized Church Planter Assessment Centers through the remainder of 2019. In 2020 and beyond, we intend to multiply our assessments into regional, and even local, expressions.

MNA 2018 Highlights: Beyond the fiscal blessings we enjoyed in 2018, we have welcomed to the MNA staff these new key leaders of ministry:

MNA Korean Ministries Coordinator TE Bill Sim. Bill will focus primarily on working with first generation PCA Korean language church pastors. He will work alongside the KALI (Korean American Leadership Initiative) leaders already serving in leadership with a focus on the second generation. KALI includes RE Alex Jun, TE Mike Park, and TE Owen Lee. Don Baret has joined us to lead MNA Media Service, leading in the development of media services for MNA as an entire organization, as well as individual MNA ministries. Don also serves as assistant director to MNA ESL Director Nancy Booher. Chris Bolton has joined our staff as MNA Operations Director. He comes to us with extensive experience in both for-profit and nonprofit organization management, along with lay leadership in a number of mission churches.

We also trust God that the new steps we are taking in providing church planting services will provide greater platforms and opportunities for growth in church renewal resourcing also. We are continuing to develop our overarching approach to church renewal. We will keep in touch with churches, networks, and presbyteries as we continue to develop church renewal resources, partnerships, and strategies.

MNA Stewardship and Finances: 2018 Progress

- **A.** Ministry Ask/Askings Giving: MNA was supported in 2018 by 1,601 churches giving $4,403,084 and 3,729 individual donors giving $2,395,556. The MNA Partnership Fund budget includes designated support for MNA program staff members. 100% of all designated gifts to MNA go to their intended project; MNA receives no administrative support from designated income. No administrative fees are taken from project support for any project coordinated by MNA. All designated gifts to MNA are used fully for the purpose designated. Church planters who do not have a strong personal PCA network require a special priority for project support as we trust God for much greater ministry among the many people groups of North America. ## APPENDIX G

Attachment 2

### MNA CHAPLAIN MINISTRIES REPORT ON 2018 ACTIVITIES

### THANKSGIVING AND PRAISE

We are thankful for the generosity of God's people as our 2018 operating expenses were covered with gifts from churches, presbyteries, individuals, and PRCC denominations. We are also thankful for the generosity of MNA's administration in managing databases, salaries, printing support, and much more. Their devotion and dedication has made a significant impact in empowering our Chaplain Ministry.

As of December 31, 2018, the PCA had a total of 209 endorsed chaplains (145 Military Chaplains and Seminary Candidates, and 64 Civilian Chaplains). The PCA continues to endorse military and civilian chaplains in a variety of settings including those of the additional 6 denominations in the Presbyterian and Reformed Commission on Chaplains (PRCC): Associate Reformed Presbyterian Church (ARPC), Korean American Presbyterian Church (KAPC), Korean Presbyterian Church in America (KPCA), Orthodox Presbyterian Church (OPC), The Reformed Presbyterian Church in North America (RPCNA), and the United Churches of North America (URCNA). I serve as the Endorser for these denominations as well as the PCA. The PRCC endorses and supports a total of 285 chaplains in all member denominations.

### 2018 HIGHLIGHTS

June 2018 Chaplains Training Conference was hosted by Smyrna PCA Church. We had over 65 Chaplains and many spouses and children attend our annual training, which was led by Kevin DeYoung and Peter Lillback. It was an amazing time of study and spiritual renewal for our Chaplains and their family members.

Civilian Chaplain Population: We are blessed to see our Civilian Chaplain ministry continue to grow. Whether they be Hospital, Bureau of Prisons, Retirement, Hospice, or Corporate Chaplains, we are encouraged to see our gracious Lord growing this ministry and Teaching Elders entering this special calling.

Chaplain Recruitment: The goal in 2018 was to add 20 Chaplains or Chaplain Candidates and we were able to add 23 Chaplains to serve our Lord within the PRCC.

309

<a id="ga47-p312"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=312 printed_page=310 -->

PRCC Staff: It is a blessing to serve with two other godly Teaching Elders and one godly Ruling Elder who make up the Chaplain Staff. TE Mack Griffith, TE Del Farris and RE Gary Hitzfeld are a true blessing and make this ministry so fulfilling. These men are outstanding servant leaders and make significant contributions to the pastoral care of our chaplains.

### CHURCH AND PRESBYTERY SUPPORT PROGRAMS

Congregational Sponsorship: It is our goal to enlist three sponsoring congregations for every full-time military and civilian chaplain. The primary purpose of the Sponsorship Program is to enlist prayer support for the chaplain, his ministry, his family, and for those he serves. The sponsoring chaplain, in turn, will provide at least three update reports per year with prayer requests to the congregation or presbytery.

Missions Conferences: More and more congregations are asking us to preach and speak at numerous mission conferences, and this has been a blessing. Several of our chaplains have also been invited to speak or preach. We encourage our ministers and congregations to ask our chaplains to come and speak. The Chaplaincy is about fulfilling the Great Commission and we deeply desire to spread the gospel of Christ.

### PLEASE JOIN IN PRAYER FOR THESE CURRENT REQUESTS

For Ministry Boldness: Pray that our Chaplains will continue to boldly  
represent our faith. Our Chaplains have the First Amendment liberty to  
boldly proclaim the gospel and we are thankful that they are standing firm.  
They are able to cooperate with other groups but without compromise. Our  
Chaplains have an excellent reputation among their peers and leaders and are  
superb at walking through the pluralistic minefields within the Chaplaincy.  
Just as Daniel was able to navigate the waters in the Court of Darius, so our  
Chaplains navigate our secular culture as they live for Christ and bring glory  
to His name. However, prayer is needed for them to continue to do so.

For Spiritual Strength: Please pray for our Chaplains as many are deploying; pray, too, for family members left behind. Also, pray for our Civilian Chaplains who pour themselves out in service to the King and face much pressure to conform to the spirit of the world.

For Increased Giving: As our ministry grows and we expand our number of Chaplains, it is critical that we increase our budget to sustain the pastoral care to our Chaplains. Our budget needs to be above $500,000 in order to

## APPENDIX H

### REPORT OF

### THE COMMITTEE ON MISSION TO THE WORLD

### TO THE FORTY-SEVENTH GENERAL ASSEMBLY

### PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA

Vision: the gospel of the kingdom advancing throughout the world ~ We want the gospel to spread throughout the world, the Church to grow, Satan's kingdom destroyed, and Christ's reign extended to the ends of the earth. Mission: making disciples among all nations ~ We are called to be obedient to the Great Commission by teaching people to follow Jesus as Lord and Savior, to be baptized, and to obey all that Jesus commands. Values: Church ~ The establishment, growth, and maturity of the Church in all our ministry efforts. Grace-based ~ Community life and ministry shaped by God's grace for us in His Son, Jesus Christ. Reformed and Covenantal ~ A ministry that is guided, inspired, and shaped by our theology. Mercy, Justice, and the Love of God ~ A love for God that is demonstrated through acts of mercy and justice.

In anticipation of God answering our prayer to raise up at least 1% of the PCA's adult members for longer-term missions for kingdom advancement, this year has been marked by intentional strategic changes:

Leadership Structure — In order to better facilitate communication and coordinate change across the organization, we have changed our leadership structure. Previously, the assistant coordinator and the international directors were the primary positions reporting to the coordinator. Moving forward, an Executive Leadership Team (ELT) of three will report to the coordinator. These positions are the chief administrative officer, senior director of field operations, and senior director of U.S. operations. Please pray for the newlyappointed leaders and that this new structure would serve our missionaries well. 316

<a id="ga47-p319"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=319 printed_page=317 -->

## APPENDIX H

Software Implementation — We gave significant time and resources to implement new financial and customer relationship management systems. From beginning to end this project was managed very capably by Kendra Jeffreys, senior director for U.S. operations, and her team. These new systems will support the growth we are anticipating. Please give thanks with us for the successful implementation of these much-needed systems.

Regional Hubs —MTW West Coast and MTW Midwest have been progressing in their service to their respective regions. Of the 100 churches that have signed up or pledged involvement in the 1% initiative, a disproportionate number have come from the West and Midwest. This is clear evidence of the fruit of the hubs' work in engaging with local congregations. MTW South Central has launched with the appointment of Jerry Gibson as director. Jerry is the former senior director of missions at Park Cities Presbyterian Church, Dallas. We are excited about his transition into this role. Lastly, a core group has formed in the Northeast/Mid-Atlantic and we anticipate a new hub in that region to launch this year. Please continue to pray for our existing hubs and those in development.

In addition to the preparations for growth, we have worked on issues related to our organizational culture and values:

We have initiated a new Reformed and Diverse Delegates group (RADD), led by Omar and Kate Ortiz, focusing on Hispanic and Latino-Americans. Our African-American RADD group has been very active in promoting missions and mentoring potential missionary candidates. We pray for the same fruit from this new Hispanic/Latino-American RADD group. Please pray for these RADD groups, and the development of an Asian-American RADD group.

We have also given much thought to valuing women in MTW. In keeping with the recommendation that was passed at the 45th General Assembly of the PCA stating, “That sessions, presbyteries and the General Assembly strive to develop, recognize, and utilize the gifts, skills, knowledge, and wisdom of godly women in the local, regional, and national church..."1, CMTW drafted this statement:

1 Lines 31-33, page 2459; Report of the Ad Interim Committee on Women Serving in the Ministry of the Church to the Forty-fifth General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America.

317

<a id="ga47-p320"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=320 printed_page=318 -->

MTW values all women as created in the image of God. Under Scripture's authority and in our doctrinal view of

ordination, we affirm that female disciples of Christ are coheirs of the kingdom, co-laborers in the work of the gospel, gifted by the Spirit as members of the body of Christ and called to use these gifts for the building up of the Church and for the extension of the Kingdom of God throughout the world.

Furthermore, the MTW community deeply needs the gifts and glory of God uniquely expressed in women. Therefore, MTW is committed to supporting and equipping our sisters in Christ as they exercise their gifts and abilities throughout MTW's global ministry as together we show and tell the gospel of God's grace.

In keeping with this statement, we affirm that women may serve in leadership roles within MTW, recognizing that only ordained elders exercise ecclesiastical authority over church plants or churches.

In addition, we asked Godly Response to Abuse in a Christian Environment (GRACE) to conduct an independent assessment of our policies and practices related to preventing and responding to behavioral misconduct in MTW, focusing especially on how women are treated. They completed their assessment and have passed on their recommendations to MTW. We are in the process of implementing those recommendations, bringing greater consistency to CMTW's statement on valuing women and our organizational culture. Please pray that we would continue to grow in demonstrating value to the many women serving with MTW.

We give thanks to God for your partnership in the gospel and count it a great privilege to participate with you in fulfilling the Great Commission. Soli Deo Gloria!

Lloyd Kim, Coordinator
