## APPENDIX H

### 2018 GLOBAL MINISTRY HIGHLIGHTS

### ASIA-PACIFIC

East Asia — WC* Covenant Theological Seminary just held its second annual graduation. MTW missionary and academic dean Tim M* looked out upon the graduates with both a sense of pride and of concern. Pride because of what the seminary has accomplished through God's grace, but concern for the trials they would face ahead. New government regulations concerning religious gatherings have been the source of personal trials for some MTW personnel. Tim recently had his visa revoked, was forced out of his previous apartment, and has been harassed by the police. All these, however, are rather mild compared to what these graduates face. The week prior to graduation Tim spoke with an American brother who comes to the seminary every year to teach a class. Since this man travels around East Asia and works with different groups, he shared how his experience at the seminary compared to other places and what was unique. He replied that he really appreciated the theological rigor and the moral courage that the leaders in at the seminary are instilling in the next generation. As Tim looked out upon the faces of the graduates he got a bit choked up during his prayer for them. “We don't know what will happen tomorrow," he prayed, "but we know our future is in His hands." Since then the church in this East Asia country has faced extensive persecution with church property destroyed, members harassed, and many imprisoned. Please pray for missionaries and national pastors in East Asia to be strengthened in their trust in the Lord and in His plans for the future. *name withheld due to sensitive ministry location

Cambodia —Khmer Christian Church (KCC) has been praying for three years for a Khmer missionary to go to Prey Thom village to minister to the families there. God heard those prayers and has answered them. Pecht and his wife, Soknee, have been called by God to serve in Prey Thom and KCC has confirmed that calling. Currently Pecht is preparing to live in Prey Thom by attending classes taught by the MTW team as well as partnering with Family Clinic to start a clinic in Prey Thom. Please pray for these ongoing preparations, for God to bring much fruit from ministry in Prey Thom village.

Perth, Australia — As the local band the Hand Me Downs took the stage at Clancy's, MTW missionary and band member Andy Shadburne looked out into the crowd to see MTW teammates, church mates, musician mates, and the mates of all those mates gathered to hear the inaugural gig of this unique band. This is where those who are in Christ are interacting with those who

319

<a id="ga47-p322"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=322 printed_page=320 -->

do not yet know they are in need of a savior. This is where the sweet aroma of Christ and life soars above the smell of pub food and beer. This is where people who might not ever connect begin to connect because of a common friend, where conversations began to form and where gospel seeds are planted and begin to germinate. The team looks forward to seeing God continue to grow those relationships and is thankful for the opportunity to connect with so many individuals. Please pray that those who are getting a whiff of the aroma of life would be compelled to seek after Christ.

Taiwan — Although she has been a Christian since childhood, J struggled for years with forgiveness issues. Studying the writing of Jonathan Edwards in a Spiritual Classics course at Christ's College, J discovered a new perspective. She wrote in a journal, “To forgive shows how much you can trust God, and it is a gift to bless us. That's what I should learn and improve over time until I can trust him through forgiveness." Please pray for the ministry of Christ's College as they seek to provide Christian education and discipleship to Taiwanese and Chinese college students.

### EUROPE

Ongoing Refugee Ministry — Over the past three years a significant ministry focus for Europe, as in other parts of the world, has been ministering to the needs of refugees. In the summer of 2016, millions of people were displaced from a variety of countries in the Middle East due to political turmoil and persecution. Most headed to Europe. While some European countries closed their borders, others welcomed refugees with open arms. The needs were great, the stories told by those who had been displaced were often heart-wrenching, and gospel opportunities abounded. God brought many people into His kingdom. What was initially deemed a refugee “crisis" has ushered in an important movement of the Holy Spirit.

Fast forward two years to 2018: Although the stream of refugees into Europe slowed to a trickle, the needs of those who have come and remain are still abundant. In that initial year, the focus was on meeting daily needs and helping displaced people simply survive their harrowing ordeal. Many governments were not set up to deal with a massive influx of people. Now many cases are being reviewed to determine whether or not these people truly meet the definition of “refugee," and thus gain legal asylum status. Many are being returned to their country of origin, where they may face persecution and even death due to having entered into a relationship with Jesus Christ during their time of sojourn on European soil. Others are given the green light to remain and enter the next phase of social integration.

320

<a id="ga47-p323"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=323 printed_page=321 -->

## APPENDIX H

This all changes the face of ministry. Field personnel now attend court  
hearings, testifying to the new-found faith of their refugee friends, pleading  
for the government to recognize the dangers that lie ahead should our  
brothers and sisters be returned to the land of their birth. The refugees are  
weary of living in limbo. Workers are weary from dealing with trauma.  
Therefore, ministry has shifted from meeting the basic needs of home,  
clothing, and food to providing care on a deeper level. Our workers in  
Athens, Greece, have opened integration houses, where refugees learn  
needed skills to become a part of Greek society. Two trauma care trainings  
were held in Europe during 2018, teaching workers how to identify not only  
trauma suffered by others, but also how to deal with the trauma they  
themselves have experienced in the process. Opportunities still abound.

Moving Leadership to “The Next Level" — With MTW's goal of mobilizing an additional 1% of the PCA's membership to world missions, at the field level we are grappling with what is needed to receive and adequately care for an expanding workforce. Trusting that God will answer our prayers for more laborers to the field, the regional leadership team has taken the following steps in 2018: Created the position of Europe mobilization coordinator to help the fields think creatively and dream of how God's kingdom in Europe could grow with an expanded work force. What are the opportunities? Needs? Interests? The sky's the limit! Created the position of women's ministry coordinator to meet the needs of the women who are serving in Europe. Over half of our field personnel are women, so this is a strategic position to ensure our personnel are reaching their potential in all areas of life. Created the position of Europe prayer coordinator to deepen the prayer life of our field personnel. Without prayerful dependence on God in all our endeavors, the work of our hands is doomed to fail. Raising up leaders: In Europe we are facing a number of significant retirements in the next two to three years. All regional directors and team leaders have been asked to actively prepare the people they oversee to eventually move into leadership positions, either in their current area or to lead new works elsewhere. During 2018 one couple was assessed for a regional leadership position, and two couples were assessed as potential team leaders. The list is growing for those who will be assessed in 2019. This is an exciting step in preparing for the future. Developing leaders: Not only do we want to appoint leaders, we also want to ensure their success as they transition into new responsibilities.

321

<a id="ga47-p324"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=324 printed_page=322 -->

A new leadership development program is being designed to assist new team leaders during the first year in their position. This program will also be open to all field personnel, as each person is a leader in his or her own ministry area. Europe Leadership Forums: Fifty people attended the MTW-Europe Leadership Forum (ELF), where the training focus was on gospel coaching. Tools were made available not only to those who have a leadership title, but also to site leaders and team members who lead ministries at the local level. The desire is to continue strengthening this training component in the future. The 2019 ELF will focus on providing church-planting training that is specific to the European context.

Please be in prayer that God would raise up laborers to join what He is doing in Europe, and that He would raise up leaders and national partners who will move this work forward in the decades to come.

### SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA

International Director — The close of 2018 marked the first year of transition for our new international director, Victor Nakah. Victor has begun a major emphasis of planting covenantal, Reformed, and Presbyterian churches and presbyteries throughout Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). This emphasis includes related ministry priorities that will bring intentionality to how we go about doing Reformed campus ministry, developing leaders, and promoting integral mission in communities we serve. He has networked with fellow African Reformed church leaders where we hope to expand churchplanting initiatives in the Congo, Malawi, and Sierra Leone. Victor has begun an initiative that we hope will make it possible to have a missionary who is focused on reaching Muslims join each of the Sub-Saharan Africa teams.

Southern Africa Reformed Mission (SARM) —February 8–9 we launched the SARM as a platform to intentionally bring resources to support MTW Southern Africa ministry priorities by creating a board comprised of missionaries and PCA church leaders committed to funding these priorities. The SARM Board will be a resource-finding board with the potential that the resourcing could also happen in both directions as functional gospel partnerships are established.

Madagascar — A short-term couple, Caleb and Whitney Wiley, joined our long-term missionary family, Bryan and Rebe McReynolds. Caleb has been developing the music ministry of their recording studio, helping Malagasy nationals put Scripture to song, then be recorded and played over regional 322

<a id="ga47-p325"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=325 printed_page=323 -->

## APPENDIX H

and national radio. Whitney has been very capably home schooling one of the McReynolds’ daughters, while also assisting in the women's ministry. Bryan and Rebe have started two fledgling church plants, one in the small village of Nosy Be where the missionary couples live, and one in a jungle setting. They know of no Reformed, covenantal, and Presbyterian church throughout the country of Madagascar. Please pray with us for this urgent need.

Uganda — MTW's Ben and Kim Church have seen fruit of their churchplanting efforts over the past several years. On December 30, the first church service was held at the newly-built Christ our Redeemer Presbyterian Church. Ben is working alongside several national partners in joint leadership at the church. At their first service, they had approximately 150 adults with 120 children in attendance. The ground-breaking service was a time of great rejoicing at our Lord's faithfulness in providing national partners, potential congregants, and financial provision for the church facilities' construction.

Ethiopia — Ethiopia ACT, the ministry started by MTW missionaries to plant churches and serve the poorest residents of Addis Ababa, continued to grow and reach more families in extreme poverty. In 2018 the ministry served more than 600 families with health care, children's education, spiritual counseling, and assistance in becoming self-sustaining. Of the 1,233 families that have been part of the project since it began, 1,129 are now able to support themselves. The team's church plant in the Suki community has grown steadily this year with 10 people making professions of faith and five baptisms. In 2019 the project is expanding into a new community, Akaki Kality, and will add 150 families to the ministry and launch a second church plant.

South Africa — In 2018 the McGintys completed their second year with REACH (Reformed Evangelical Anglican Church of South Africa) student ministry at the University of Cape Town (UCT). Since this ministry was only formed recently, the McGintys' focus has been on laying the foundation for future ministry—establishing relationships, investing in student leadership, and, of course, sharing the gospel. REACH has also launched a church plant connected to the student ministry at UCT. This church grew numerically in 2018, capitalizing on synergy from the student ministry. Pamela McGinty was also involved in another new and necessary ministry that started in 2018: a biblical counseling ministry with national scope. Biblical Counseling South

323

<a id="ga47-p326"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=326 printed_page=324 -->

Africa was started in partnership with REACH S.A. and U.S.-based CCEF (Christian Counseling & Educational Foundation). The purpose is to equip lay and pastoral counselors for the churches in South Africa..

### AMERICAS

Seminario Biblico Reformado – Arequipa — We are grateful to see growth at the Seminario Biblico Reformado in Arequipa, Peru. The seminary just concluded its first academic year and registered its hundredth student, praise the Lord! The first group of students has completed two thirds of their program, and we have recently launched the newest extension of the seminary in Spain. Unfortunately, one of our church plants, La Roca, had to close its doors in the fall, but God provided amidst the change. Since the closing of the church, we have been able to serve multiple churches represented in the seminary. Our team participated in marriage conferences, church anniversary services, funerals, and regular preaching. We are thankful that Seminario Biblico Reformado has already touched the lives of over 100 students in Peru, Venezuela, and Spain. We look forward to seeing how the Lord continues to work through the seminary.

RUF – Bogota — MTW missionary Peter Dishman continues to see progress and traction in the RUF ministry at the University of Colombia in Bogota. In August, Peter and his team handed out 6,000 academic calendars. They had 1,086 students sign up for more information on English clubs and 271 for more information on Bible studies. They continue to have weekly large group meetings and small group studies covering a range of topics from the Jesus Storybook Bible to Theology Club. Three of their students in leadership grew significantly this past year by leading small groups and caring for the group members. We are grateful for the work the Lord continues to do in this ministry, and we pray this is only the beginning of His work.

Global Distance Education — Our Global Education team continued to flourish throughout 2018. MTW missionary Carla Stevens developed courses in Christian Education and traveled throughout the world to teach seminars. Missionaries Quentin and Karen Nantz worked alongside Carla, helping develop the courses and assisting in the establishment of Christian schools. The Nantzes are also focusing on developing an online course, which would enable MTW to reach even more students. We are grateful that they are receiving positive feedback from the courses. Please pray that their roles in education would impact many for the kingdom

8. Regarding MTW'$ 2017 Financial Audit: That the Committee of Commissioners reviewed the financial audit for calendar year ending December 31, 2017. They also noted per CMTW's minutes that CMTW had accepted the audit.

9. That Overture 24 from Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery "Add Constitutional Precedence Statement to Policy Manuals" be answered with reference to the recommendation from the Administrative Committee regarding Overture 24.

10. That Overture 41 from Heritage Presbytery, "Direct CMTW to Amend its Guidelines to Implement CMTW’s Statement on Valuing Women in MTW,' so that only Ordained Elders Will Be Allowed to Serve in the Roles of Team Leader, Regional Director, and International Director within MTW," (p. 693) be answered in the negative. With the following grounds recorded as part of the motion.

Grounds: In formulating and finalizing its “Statement on Valuing Women," CMTW carefully considered the report on the ad interim committee to the 45th

330

<a id="ga47-p333"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=333 printed_page=331 -->

## APPENDIX H

General Assembly and believes that its statement on valuing women in MTW is wholly consistent with the ad interim report in all material respects.

Mission to World, CMTW, and the General Assembly have approved unordained men to the roles of team leader, country director, and regional director since 1983 and at least 3 women since around 2006. We have identified at least 35 unordained leaders appointed to these positions since

2003. CMTW and GA have never required these positions be held exclusively by ordained elders.

MTW teams vary extensively across the globe. While the ultimate aim of all our teams is to plant and revitalize churches, not all of our teams have ordained elders engaged directly in planting churches. Some teams are focused on facilitative church planting where our missionaries work alongside ordained national partners who are leading churches and church plants. Others are focused on university ministries (Christ's College team in Taiwan), medical ministries, mercy ministries (Ethiopia), education ministries, etc. to make disciples who fill local churches and church plants. In some cases there are a variety of different ministries all under the umbrella of one team. The overture would unnecessarily restrict unordained men and women from serving in roles that do not require ordination.

The overture if passed would immediately affect 19 unordained missionaries who are serving in these roles across the globe as well as their teams. These leaders would be removed from their positions, receive less remuneration, and would have to find new roles on the team. It would also require taking 19 ordained missionaries out of their current ministry roles to take their places.

CMTW and the coordinator are committed to working with those whose consciences are affected by women or unordained men serving in leadership in non-ecclesial roles over (ordained) men. We want to move forward together in a manner that does not hinder the work of the Kingdom.

The principle that unordained leaders defer matters of the church to ordained leaders in line authority has been MTW's practice for many years. Women and unordained men in leadership over TE church planters routinely defer matters related to the church to other ordained supervisors. While this practice necessarily involves line-drawing, in practice this line-drawing has

331

<a id="ga47-p334"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=334 printed_page=332 -->

not proved to be an unsurmountable problem, and we pledge to continue to ensure that church matters be referred to the proper ordained authorities.

The authority given to team leaders for spiritual care of their members does not necessitate ordination. Spiritual care can be given by unordained believers. Team leaders can also delegate to others to provide spiritual care as is appropriate.

Finally, while CMTW has non-voting women advisors, CMTW is not proposing the addition of women to serve on CMTW through this statement.

Respectfully submitted, TE Mark Bates, Chairman Committee on Mission to the World

## APPENDIX I

### REPORT OF THE

### PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA

### FOUNDATION, INC.

### TO THE FORTY-SEVENTH GENERAL ASSEMBLY

### OF THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA

The PCA Foundation is pleased to report that, by God's grace, the PCA Foundation's ministry was once again blessed during 2018. We are pleased to see how the Lord continues to help the PCA Foundation facilitate generosity to advance God's Kingdom. Total gifts to the PCA Foundation during 2018 were $11.8 million. We are pleased to report that the PCA Foundation distributed, or granted to ministry, $14.4 million during 2018. Distributions to PCA churches were $4.7 million, distributions to PCA Committees and Agencies were $2.1 million, and distributions to other Christian ministries were $7.6 million. We continue to look for opportunities to work with PCA churches and their members, and are desirous of helping individuals and their families fulfill their stewardship responsibilities and carry out their charitable desires. The 2018 distributions and grants to ministry by the PCA Foundation were as follows: Mission to the World $ 458,000 Mission to North America 290,000 Committee on Discipleship Ministries 68,000 Administrative Committee 20,000 RBI-Ministerial Relief 195,000 Reformed University Ministries 279,000 Covenant College 307,000 Covenant Theological Seminary 172,000 PCA Foundation 143,000 Ridge Haven 123,000 Total Committees & Agencies 2,055,000

PCA Churches 4,708,000 Other Christian Ministries 7,674,000 Total $14,437,000

337

<a id="ga47-p340"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=340 printed_page=338 -->

The PCA Foundation's total assets were $86.4 million as of December 31,

2018. This compares to $93.1 million as of December 31, 2017. The primary reasons that total assets declined $6.7 million during 2018 were grant distributions exceeding gifts to the PCA Foundation to fund accounts by $2.6 million and asset valuation decreases of $3.9 million due to the 2018 yearend financial market declines. Much of what the Foundation does results in gifts coming into the Foundation and going right back out as distributions and grants to ministries within a relatively short period of time – often within the same or the following year. Therefore, the PCA Foundation may realize significant amounts as both gifts and distributions in a given year, and total assets may stay about the same, or experience substantial increases or decreases from year to year.

The PCA Foundation has and continues to make significant progress in serving members and friends of the PCA. Over the last 20 years, total assets have grown from $20.0 million to $86.4 million. This total asset balance provides a sound base for future financial support of PCA Churches, PCA Committees and Agencies, and other Christian ministries.

Coincidental with the growth of its assets over the last 20 years, the PCA Foundation received $207.9 million in gifts, and made distributions to ministries totaling $151.9 million.

During 2018 the PCA Foundation continued its increased intentional marketing to individuals and families, churches, presbyteries, and ministries. The PCA Foundation rebranded its look with a new logo, website, and marketing materials in 2016, during which time it also began using various social networking platforms to introduce its services to individuals and churches.

The donor portal, which went live in 2016, continues in its increasing popularity with donors. The donor portal allows PCA Foundation donors to access their account information online, from which they can also recommend grant distributions from their accounts.

The PCA Foundation became fully self-supported in 2000. The Foundation does not participate in the PCA's Partnership Shares or Ministry Ask Programs, nor does it rely on the financial support of churches to help underwrite its operating budget. Rather, its operations are funded primarily by fees and earnings on accounts, and by some charitable contributions from a small number of individuals and families, including current and former

338

<a id="ga47-p341"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=341 printed_page=339 -->

## APPENDIX I

PCA Foundation Board Members. Prior to becoming self-supported, a significant amount of its operating expenses were underwritten by some of the PCA Committees and Agencies.

Because the main focus of the PCA Foundation is not on raising funds for its own operations, or for any other particular ministry, it has a unique opportunity and niche within the PCA. Our ministry is providing charitable financial services and vehicles to help Christians carry out their stewardship responsibilities and charitable desires. We facilitate generosity to advance God's kingdom. Our most popular service is the Advise & Consult Fund (a donor-advised fund). We also offer endowments, charitable trusts, bequest processing and estate design to individuals and families, as well as Designated Funds for Churches and Presbyteries.

Since the PCA Foundation is self-supported it is “donor driven," which means that we work on the donor's agenda, not our own, or that of any other ministry. Therefore, the timing and amounts of distributions and to which ministry are determined by the donors themselves, not the PCA Foundation. We provide charitable services to individuals without pressuring them to give to the PCA Foundation for its own operations, or to any other particular ministry.

The PCA Foundation will continue to strive to effectively meet the needs of its present and future donors, as well as those of the PCA: its churches, presbyteries, Committees, and Agencies. By God's grace, the PCA Foundation will be able to do so.

In July 2018, I informed the PCA Foundation Board of my intention to retire on June 30, 2019, after more than 21 years as president. I am thankful for the opportunity to have been able to serve the Lord, the PCA, and our donors since 1998.

On March 1, 2019, the PCA Foundation Board elected Timothy W. Townsend to succeed me as president, effective July 1, 2019. Please pray that he will be successful as the next president, and will find joy in serving in his new calling. Also, please pray for the Board and Staff of the Foundation as they seek to continue leading the PCA Foundation successfully into the future. The PCA Foundation is financially sound, and is postured well for continued growth.

### APPENDIXJ

### REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF

### PCA RETIREMENT & BENEFITS

### TO THE FORTY-SEVENTH GENERAL ASSEMBLY

### OF THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA

We are pleased to present the 2018 Annual Report on behalf of the Board of Directors and Staff of PCA Retirement & Benefits.

As I begin writing this, my twelfth President's Annual Report, I do so with mixed feelings. Some of you may have heard that PCA Retirement & Benefits (RBI) recently announced the beginning of a transition process to find the next President. After consultations with RBI's Board of Directors, we determined the search process should begin immediately. I have given your Board my commitment to remain in this position until it is clear that God's leader for this organization has been named and is prepared to assume the position of President.

You should know my love for ministry partners who serve in the PCA ministries and my vision for this work have not diminished. It's not unusual for those who consider retirement to do so because the former "fire in the belly" started smoldering. I can assure you this is not how I feel about the ministry of RBI! Why then would I want to leave a ministry I love so much?

There are several reasons why I believe entering this period of change is good and necessary. First, I have no intention of disengaging from a ministry of love and care for those who serve the church as our pastors and employees. I'm confident God will surely guide my path into work that reflects the desires of my heart! Second, entering this period of leadership transition is simply good stewardship. Often, senior leaders remain in their positions too long. I believe an example of good stewardship is to properly hand the job to the next incumbent at the right time with excellence. So, "just as a good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children" (Proverbs 13:22), a good leader should steward his transition with supreme care. Finally, I believe denominational leaders have an awesome responsibility to prepare the next generation for important positions of leadership in the church, such as RBI's presidency. Every participant in any of the PCA's benefit plans deserves our very best and we will do all that is possible to deliver that standard. 342

<a id="ga47-p345"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=345 printed_page=343 -->

### APPENDIXJ

There is one more area of change I'd like to mention in this report, which is the retirement of TE Bob Clarke. Bob has served RBI for 13 years as a member of the Board of Directors and for the past 10 years as the Director of Ministerial Relief. During Bob's tenure with RBI he has faithfully served the widows of our pastors, overseen the development of the Retirement Readiness survey, and grown Ministerial Relief by adding needed new ministries such as ServantCare and Cherish. Bob has been a faithful partner in ministry and he will be greatly missed. We expect to announce his replacement in early April of 2019. Please pray that God would continue to bless the work of our hands as we navigate this important transitional period.

Given all of the changes mentioned above, let me conclude this section of the annual report by stating what will not change. When RBI's Board of Directors formed the President Search Committee, it was done with the expectation that this committee's primary goal would be to find a candidate who would preserve and grow RBI's stated Mission, Vision and Core Values. Clearly, finding a candidate with the requisite technical skills is very important, but preserving the relational and ministry-minded culture of this organization is vital. I am thankful and happy to say the Board of Directors and members of RBI's staff all fully support this objective. Praise the Lord!!

Financial Market Update If you thought making money in the stock market looked easy after 2017, this past year (2018) was a reminder that risk over the short run remains an enduring challenge. Stocks (as measured by the S&P 500) experienced a near ceaseless experience of continuing new highs in 2017. The new year was quickly interrupted by news of tariff wars and stocks didn't really find their stride until the beginning of the second quarter. Just when it seemed like we were experiencing the second leg of our prior years’ experience (insert sounds of champagne corks popping), pain and misery became our new friend as the market unmercifully began a swan dive at the end of the third quarter. By the end of the year most markets posted negative returns which was very unsettling.

As investors who are very interested in achieving reasonable returns, how do we understand this post Great Recession recovery? For what it's worth, here are my thoughts at this time... First, the U.S economy has finally achieved the technical status of "full employment". This has long been the Fed's objective and there are many implications for this status which include worries about wage inflation and a rising quit rate (resigning employees seeking higher pay).

343

<a id="ga47-p346"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=346 printed_page=344 -->

The Fed has been regularly increasing short term interest rates. This monetary policy together with the reversal of the QE (Quantitative Easing) program is having a tightening impact on the economy. Recently the Fed has declared they are maintaining a more neutral policy with respect to higher interest rates and I believe lower interest rates are the new normal. Growth rates in the U.S. are likely to slow modestly. Contributing factors are the economic slowdown in China, stagnant growth in Europe, the Brexit disaster in the U.K., the ebbing favorable impact of the U.S. corporate tax cut, and the divided U.S. Congress which will neutralize fiscal policy impacts.

All this is to say the biggest growth we've recently experienced is behind us. This recovery is now 10 years old, having produced an average annual return of 13.12% for the S&P 500. We should experience more moderate growth in the years ahead given the factors presented above, and there seems to be no material evidence of a potential recession yet on the horizon.

Finally, I'm excited to report that in partnership with Women's Ministry of PCA Committee on Discipleship Ministries, RBI will be introducing a new counseling ministry for pastors' wives called Cherish. God has tremendously blessed us with the necessary resources to begin this vital ministry. It is our greatest hope that God will use this ministry to bring hope and healing to hurting Teaching Elder families across the PCA. Thank you for your support of PCA Retirement & Benefits. Through your participation in the Retirement Plan, Group Insurance products and Ministerial Relief, we are able to sustain programs that encourage and support our PCA churches and employees.

Summary of 2018 Operations Total PCA Retirement Plan assets under management decreased by 3.6% from $576,949,747 to $556,375,106. This decrease can be attributed to outflows (withdrawals and distributions) and comparative market performance over the prior year. The PCA Retirement Plan continues to be the employee benefit plan with the largest amount of participation with over 7500 retirement accounts at year-end 2018.

Participation results for the various PCA insurance benefit plans offered by RBI remained strong with an over growth of 2% in insurance participation. For the year, participation and volume increased in the PCA Long Term Disability Plan and the combined PCA Life Insurance Plans, with little change in participation in both the PCA Vision Plan and the PCA Dental Plan.

## APPENDIX K

### REPORT OF

### REFORMED UNIVERSITY FELLOWSHIP

### TO THE FORTY-SEVENTH GENERAL ASSEMBLY

### OF THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA

### INTRODUCTION

Ministry to colleges represents an important part of the mission of the Presbyterian Church in America. The college years have increasingly become a time for questioning authority, scrutinizing absolutes, throwing out old premises, and reinventing the self. Students must learn to navigate the milieu of converging thought, and Reformed University Fellowship is thankful to be part of this unfolding campus narrative to reach students for Christ and equip them to serve. The passion and vigor of college students have proved, over the last 200 years, to affect the church globally, significantly engaging the world with mission and purpose. The story of redemption playing out is bigger than any story that we can imagine.

Reformed University Fellowship goes to the campus with a fixed theology (The Westminster Standards) and a flexible methodology that allows us to contextualize in order to suit various campus personalities and demographics. We are not limited in how and where we preach the Gospel, and we know that a large percentage of people come to faith in Jesus between the age of 18 and 25.

To engage the current academic culture, Reformed University Fellowship sends ordained PCA ministers to serve on the college campus, preach the gospel of Christ, build Christ's Church, and ultimately prepare students to live all of life under the Lordship of Christ. This is a concrete expression of our commitment to our covenant children and our obedience to the Great Commission, to reach students for Christ and equip them to serve.

The Permanent Committee for Reformed University Fellowship wishes to thank all of our churches, presbyteries, and the General Assembly for their oversight, financial support, prayers, and encouragement for our campus ministers, staff, and interns, who have served on 163 campuses across America.

348

<a id="ga47-p351"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=351 printed_page=349 -->

## APPENDIX K

### REFORMED UNIVERSITY FELLOWSHIP

Reformed University Fellowship (RUF) offers the truth of God's Word to students who are searching. By working within the context of the Church, we follow Christ's leadership as He builds His Kingdom. Students are instructed in Evangelism and Missions, Growth in Grace, Fellowship and Service, and a Biblical World-and-Life View. An ordained PCA minister leads each RUF, actively working to accomplish goals in these four major areas. RUF strengthens the Church by reaching students who may not know Christ, as well as equipping those who know Him to serve, and to love Jesus for a lifetime. (See Attachment 1 for a list of RUF, RUF-I, and Global campus ministers, campuses served, and Presbytery committees.)

### REFORMED UNIVERSITY FELLOWSHIP INTERNATIONAL

We began the semester with RUF-I Training in Dallas, TX. RUF-I staff are with all other RUF staff at July Training, with a separate training in the winter, which is RUF-I specific. We had approximately 30 RUF-I staff together for 3 days of fellowship and training. Dr. Denis LaClare, from Bridges International, spoke on Engaging International Student Cultures and Engaging and Understanding Honor-Shame Cultures. It was exciting to have Chad Brewer and his family there with us in order for the RUF-I staff to spend time getting to know them. Chad will assume his new role as the Assistant Coordinator for RUF-I/G on June 1. Currently we have 16 RUF-I ministries and we ask that you pray for Chad's transition as well as new opportunities to see this ministry expand. We were able to assess two RUF- I candidates, one of whom will be filling the role as RUF-I Campus Minister at Auburn University, which is has been vacant this year.

### REFORMED UNIVERSITY FELLOWSHIP GLOBAL

Four of our six RUF-Global Campus Ministers (affiliations with MTW and SERGE) were able to attend RUF Staff Training in December. Currently, we have staff in Malaysia, Ukraine, Czech Republic, Senegal, Mexico City, and Colombia. Chad Brewer and John Pearson visited RUF-G staff in Bogota, Colombia, in January and spent two days teaching over 30 South American Pastors and Campus Staff RUF's Philosophy of Ministry. It was an exciting time to see how God is using RUF in the lives of so many Colombian college students. Conversations are currently happening with teams across the globe, who have expressed interest in affiliating with RUF in hopes of more effectively reaching college students.

### MINISTRY DISTINCTIVES

Weekly large group, small groups, and one-on-one staff-student meetings provide the structure for campus ministry. Each kind of meeting is essential

349

<a id="ga47-p352"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=352 printed_page=350 -->

in ministering to college students. In large group meetings, the truth is taught through preaching the good news of Jesus and corporate worship. Small groups focus on study, prayer, and fellowship, and many are led by junior and senior students, under the direction of the campus minister and interns. One-on-one meetings between students and staff members offer in-depth discipleship, evangelistic encounters, and accountability in trust-confidence relationships, as well as counseling. RUF emphasizes the development of a biblical world-and-life view. As students learn to think biblically, they will make a lasting difference in the Church and the world. A key distinctive of RUF is its connection to the Church. Through exhortation by their campus minister, attendance with friends at local churches, involvement in campus community, and exposition of Biblical truth, college students learn to love the Church and develop a lifelong commitment to involvement with God's people. RUF provides a bridge maintaining (or establishing) connection to the Church as students make the transitions from home to college to work and family life. RUF does not exist for the purpose of perpetuating a campus ministry, but in order to grow the church.

### CAMPUS INTERNS AND STAFF

Launched in 1980, the Intern Program has trained over 700 interns. In the last 28 years the program has grown at a rate of 13% per year. Nearly 161 young men and women (all recent college graduates) are currently working directly with a campus minister to receive on-the-job training in evangelism, small group leadership, and one-on-one ministry. While interns minister to college students, they also participate in a study program focusing on biblical and theological training. After their internship with Reformed University Fellowship, interns move into both vocational ministry and the broader marketplace with a deepened understanding of God's Word and experience in His service. The campus intern, as well as campus staff, is equipped to be "an instrument for noble purposes, made holy, useful to the Master and prepared to do any good work" (II Timothy 2:21). (See Attachment 2.)

The Campus Staff program within RUF exists to provide a long-term vocational ministerial position for women who desire to work on the college campus. While most of our Campus Staff come directly from serving two years as an RUF intern, we have begun expanding outside of that channel to bring in qualified candidates in an effort to meet the growing demand on campus. (See Attachment 2.)

In 2018, the Campus Staff department hired six new full-time staff, and three part-time staff to bring the overall number of staff to 28.

### SUMMER CONFERENCE

Summer Conference 2018 – In May 2018, Reformed University Fellowship hosted its 38th RUF Summer Conference at Laguna Beach Christian Retreat Center in Panama City Beach, Florida. In our three weeks of conferences this year, we hosted 2,158 students and 461 staff and their families. Last year Summer Conference large group speakers addressed the topic of Justification, one of the principles of RUF Philosophy of Ministry. Week One Dates: May 7–12, Speaker: Rev James Forsyth, Senior Pastor, McLean Presbyterian Church, McLean, VA. Week Two Dates: May 14–19, Speaker: Rev Chad Scruggs, Associate Pastor, Park Cities Presbyterian Church, Dallas, TX. Week Three Dates: May 21-26, Speaker: Rev John Stone, Former Assistant Coordinator, RUF, Knoxville, TN. The Summer Conference schedule included seminars in the morning, afternoon fellowship and recreation, and large group in the evening followed by small group discussions and fellowship. Total income including scholarships granted was $843,429. Expenses totaled $837,949 including scholarship refund.

Summer Conference 2019 – May 2019 registration opened March 1, and over 2,500 students are projected to attend this year. The 2019 cost per student is $375. Large group speakers will cover the topic of Sanctification. The format for this summer schedule will be similar to last year: seminars in the morning, afternoon recreation, and evening large group, followed small groups and fellowship. Week One Dates: May 6-11, Speaker Rev Hunter Bailey, Planting Pastor, Christ Community Church, Fayetteville, AR. Week Two Dates: May 13-18, Speaker Rev Shawn Slate, Senior Pastor, Redeemer Presbyterian Church, Knoxville, TN. Week Three Dates: May 19-24, Rev Russ Whitfield, Pastor, Grace Mosaic, Washington, DC, and Director of Cross-Cultural Ministry, RUF.

### WIVES RETREAT

Ninety-one RUF Campus Minister wives descended on the city of New Orleans the weekend of January 17-20. It is the largest attended Wives Weekend to date. RUF Wives enjoyed the sites and sounds of New Orleans, and of course the food. Paige Brown and Rev. Reyn Cabinte were this year's weekend speakers. Wives also enjoyed time together in Prayer Groups and Area dinners. We are extremely grateful for the role wives play in RUF's ministry to college students, and Wives Weekend plays a vital role in encouraging them in their marriages and ministry.

### STAFF TRAINING

In 2018, the three full weeks of training for field staff included orientation for new interns and new campus ministers. This in-depth training is a distinctive of the ministry and provides philosophical, practical, and reflective instruction to RUF campus ministers, interns, and staff. We have Dr. Sandy Willson teaching on leadership at 2019 July Staff Training.

### RUF CAMPUS MINISTER ASSESSMENT

In December of 2006, RUF held its first Campus Minister Assessment. Since that time, Assessment has been held twice a year, in February and July. During Assessment, candidates are interviewed by former and senior RUF ministers and some of their wives. The prospective campus ministers complete a personality profile, preach and demonstrate small group leadership, and engage with assessors in a marriage and family interview, along with other activities designed to help RUF evaluate each applicant. We assess approximately 25 candidates a year.

### GROWTH

2018 was another year of growth as RUF partnered with presbyteries to start four new campus; University of Texas-Dallas RUF-I, RUF-I at Johns Hopkins, RUF-I at Columbia University, RUF at Indiana University of Pennsylvania. This growth placed RUF ministries over 163 campuses in 38 states and in 60 Presbyteries.

Reformed University Fellowship continues to grow with 7 new ministries to begin in 2019.

### RUF'S VISION FOR THE CHURCH

RUF continues to be a pipeline for leadership in the PCA. Currently over 90 former RUF Campus Ministers are serving our church as church planters, pastors, associate pastors, assistant pastors, and denominational staff. Thousands of RUF Alumni are serving in the church enforcing the fact that RUF is not just about perpetuating campus ministry but about enriching the Church. We continue to assist in the planting of churches through our church planting initiative program.

### CONCLUSION

God is at work through the ministry of RUF. RUF strives to engage culture and carry out the kingdom priorities of the Church. God brings together students and ministers from many different walks of life to accomplish His purposes. Each person influenced by Reformed University Fellowship will in turn influence many other people in the course of his or her life. The Church is strengthened as students learn to love and seek out the Church, and are trained to serve as future church leaders.

## APPENDIX L

### RIDGE HAVEN

Brevard, NC – Cono, IA

### REPORT

### TO THE FORTY-SEVENTH GENERAL ASSEMBLY

### OF THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA

As mentioned in our Budget Report, it has been an amazing year capping off nine straight years of wonderful ministry, and phenomenal growth. We are blessed and humbled that, this year alone, over 100 churches and 30 college ministries have come to Ridge Haven. For the first time we hosted over 5,000 guests this summer. Adding to that encouragement, we had even more attend our year-round programs. We finished the year with the total guest tally of over 10,000. In addition, we hosted almost 200 at our new RH Cono campus in Iowa. What a year indeed.

Each year we consider the possibility that Ridge Haven's growth may begin to plateau. Yet to our astonishment, the Lord, through our churches, seems to say, "keep going, keep growing." In the past several years we have completed a number of expansion projects to accommodate our growth. First, we remodeled Robeson meeting hall to host 275-300 guests. Then we built additional lodging facilities to accommodate up to 700. This resulted in a pressing need to build a dining hall that was able to hold this drastically increased number. Thankfully, the Lord blessed us with our new Jolly Dining Hall. The old dining hall building was then reconfigured to provide another meeting space for 200 guests. Then we believed that once Jolly Dining Hall was completed, we could take a breather from new projects in Brevard for a while. But it became apparent this past year that we are not done growing yet.

Now that our Brevard campus can lodge and feed 700+ guests, we need more facilities for indoor meeting space. This will balance out the capacities of our campus, and allow us to continue to grow. We love our large outdoor Barnes Activity Pavilion that can host 600-700 in the spring, summer and early fall. But as one group that used it this November commented, “it is just too cold in November, put us on the wait list for October." Sadly, this past year we had to turn away two large groups in October and November for lack of indoor meeting space.

370

<a id="ga47-p373"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=373 printed_page=371 -->

## APPENDIX L

We are thrilled that we have already hosted over 2,000 visitors at Ridge Haven Brevard just during this year's winter season. Ironically, it was not too long ago that we questioned the value of hosting events year-round. Most summer camps function seasonally, and we wrestled with the idea of following that model of ministry. But the Lord was clear at the time that there was value in our off season retreat efforts. And even if the numbers were small, that we should partner with our PCA churches to support relational ministry growth through retreats. Additionally, we saw the value and evangelical potential to host other Christian organizations. To our delight, our “off-season" has become just as busy as the summer camp season. What a special thrill it is to see groups of college students and young adults, the next generation of leadership in the PCA, gathering to learn, to worship, and to relax together in the beauty of God's creation.

To give a picture of what the retreat season now looks like: while writing this report on Saturday March 23, there are two college groups on campus (one of which is a ministry to international students), a PCA church's youth group, and a PCA men's retreat group. The sun is out, it is a very comfortable 55 degrees and it is beautiful. What a blast. But, just a month ago we had multiple church groups here and it rained the whole weekend. Don't get me wrong, the groups had a great time. We received some of our best surveys. One attendee left the note, “RH is a beautiful campus. I enjoyed my stay even with the rainy weather. The paths were well maintained despite the wet season." Though we are grateful for the gracious attitudes of our guests, when the high is 45 degrees and the rain is relentless, everyone on campus needs at least a few hours inside, at the very least for their meeting times. Unfortunately, when we have many groups on campus, meeting space is a premium and we end up forced to use outdoor space such as the Barnes Center. As mentioned, we have had groups recently opt to be put on a wait list for the sake of reserving some indoor meeting space.

Thus, we have enthusiastically started planning and raising funds to build an indoor multipurpose building that can be used as a gym and large meeting space, and eventually will include our camp store, a coffee shop, and smaller meeting rooms. We feel confident that the right next step is for us to build upon the growing year-round ministry in Brevard. We are trusting that the Lord will bless this new building project as He has so abundantly provided with our others building efforts.

As you know, through the generosity of our churches in Iowa, we expanded our ministry to Cono, Iowa, last year. We ran two weeks of summer camp at

371

<a id="ga47-p374"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=374 printed_page=372 -->

Cono and had phenomenally positive feedback from the children, youth, and adult leaders that attended. In fact, many of last year's attendees have signed up to return this year. There are so many small PCA churches in the Midwest and our goal is to provide a space where these children and youth can convene and be encouraged by the testimony of staff and by connecting with other students. One PCA pastor from Missouri validated this effort by telling us, "We feel like a complete island out here. Our kids are used to doing things on their own; it would be so encouraging for them to interact with other kids in the denomination!" We have four weeks of camp planned for 2019. While we are thankful to extend our camp offerings this year, we have a tremendously long way to go before we can fully utilize the Cono facility that God has so wonderfully provided.

We hope that Cono can be like Brevard, a year-round operation. To get our summer camp ministry started at Cono in 2018, we had to quickly construct six camper cabins to hold a total of 72 guests each week. In order to expand our camp capacity and to include spring and fall retreat services, we have two large and expensive mandatory maintenance projects to complete. First, we must install sprinkler systems in the existing lodging facilities, a statemandated requirement. Once installed, we will be able to handle over 300 campers each week. Secondly, we need extensive repair work for the sewage system. Humanly speaking, both projects feel like huge hurdles, but we are trusting the Lord as we seek to raise the two million dollars in necessary funds.

In our increasingly secular culture, we praise the Lord that there are many camps on mission to grow gospel truths in the hearts and minds of the next generation. While we share a common goal with these organizations nationwide, we also “do ministry" quite differently from many. Ridge Haven programs place emphasis on mentoring through its staff and group activities, and not just through entertaining activities. We want children, youth, and adults to interact with the Lord and with each other, and truly grow in their spiritual walk.

We center our activities and schedules around authentic relationship building. The games and activities we choose to facilitate focus on group interaction, rather than simply personal enjoyment. One of the reasons we discontinued running our zipline was that it was too individually focused. There is a time and place for personal challenge, but in the limited time we have with campers over the course of a week, we want them to leave camp inspired and equipped to walk with Jesus. Research continues to show that foundational beliefs take root most through relationship building.

372

<a id="ga47-p375"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=375 printed_page=373 -->

## APPENDIX L

Studies also show that 80% of the decisions that are made for the Lord come during the formative years of childhood and youth. What a God given opportunity we have – to meet, mentor, and minister to our covenant children each camping season. And not to be forgotten is the ministry training and experience that is being provided to the nearly 100 interns and counselors that work as year-round and summer staff to support our programs. Trained and mentored themselves through our programs, work experience, and campus pastors, these sharp young adults are the future.

It is worth noting that our year-round expansion is not aimed at financial gain, although our growth has helped us continue to keep our camp costs low. As mentioned, many camping facilities operate seasonally because the cost of year-round operation often exceeds their income. Yet, Ridge Haven's ability to partner with our churches – many of whom are too small to have youth staff – is too important of a calling to dismiss. Indeed, due to the generosity of our churches and donors, we also offer camp scholarships, and even free camp for some inner-city ministries.

God has provided us with a place for year-round spiritual growth and development, and so we should continue to grow. Thankfully, the Lord has also given us the confidence that He wants us to keep it up with the incredibly increasing numbers He has brought us. And so, we continue in faith, and with your prayers and blessings.

4. That February 23, 2020, be a day for our churches to pray for the ministries of Ridge Haven.

### COOPERATIVE MINISTRIES COMMITTEE

### TO THE FORTY-SEVENTH GENERAL ASSEMBLY

### OF THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA

### THE FUNCTIONS OF THE COOPERATIVE MINISTRIES COMMITTEE

The CMC is unique in that all ten of the chairmen of the General Assembly Permanent Committees and Agency Boards, along with the Chief Administrative Officers of the General Assembly Permanent Committees and Agencies are all voting members. Also the present Moderator and five immediate past Moderators of the General Assembly are advisory members. The Cooperative Ministries Committee was formed by the 34th General Assembly in 2006, as a result of the Strategic Planning process, to serve as a forum for advancing inter-agency cooperation, collaboration, or conflict resolution (RAO 7-3.f, h), to monitor or evaluate the standards of effectiveness and efficiency of Permanent Committees and Agencies (RAO 7-3.g), and to engage in long-range planning (RAO 7-3.c).

The CMC is a consultative body within the PCA structure. It cannot make recommendations directly to the General Assembly. From 2006 to 2017 the CMC could make recommendations to Committees and Agencies, which would consider, approve, amend, or negate such recommendations for matters that required Assembly action. In 2017 the Forty-fifth General Assembly amended RAO 7-3.c to remove the CMC's ability even to recommend to Committees and Agencies matters that require Assembly action. RAO 7-3.c now requires that any matters dealt with in the CMC that necessitate Assembly action can only come to the Assembly via overtures from Presbyteries (M45GA, 2017, p. 51).

Over the past years, the CMC has worked to “facilitate integrated long-range planning that supports progress toward the overall mission and ministry of the PCA."

### MEETINGS OF THE COOPERATIVE MINISTRIES COMMITTEE

The Cooperative Ministries Committee met twice since the last General Assembly, on September 10, 2018, 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. and on January 23, 2019, 9:00 a.m. to 2:15 p.m., both at the Crowne Plaza near the Atlanta Airport. A fellowship dinner was held the night before each meeting. 374

Principles of Coordinator Unity

“Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity." Psalm 133:1 ESV)

As Coordinators and Presidents, we believe our mutual fellowship should represent the reality of our union with the Lord Jesus Christ (John 17:20-23). As we serve in positions of leadership, we hope the priority of our deep and abiding relationships with each other will be a visible reminder of gospel oneness, a display to all who observe the reality of the love of the Lord Jesus for his people.

In order to pursue this goal and move forward in love, we pledge ourselves to the following. Our desire is that gospel and covenantal unity among the elected leaders of the denomination will contribute to a greater gospel and covenantal unity among the elders of the denomination.

“...Walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" (Ephesians 4:1-3 ESV).

“Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear" (Ephesians 4:29 ESV).

We pledge to assist each other in pursuing a deeper understanding of Christ in the gospel. Gospel unity rejoices in and promotes the truth as revealed by God in his Word. Unity is not sameness. Though we are united by common ordination vows, our ministry experiences and priorities are often different. We pledge to pray regularly for each other and the ministries we represent. We pledge to communicate regularly with each other regarding the blessings we enjoy and the challenges we face in the lives of our families and ministries. We pledge to make our corporate gatherings a priority. When circumstances prevent us from attending, we will inform the group and ask to be excused. We will later seek to know what happened in our absence.

378

<a id="ga47-p381"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=381 printed_page=379 -->

## APPENDIX M

We pledge to avoid a root of bitterness by communicating to each other quickly and directly when we are offended. We pledge to help each other understand better God's Word and promote the doctrine contained in the Word as summarized in the Westminster Standards. We will seek to understand fully the views of another before we seek to correct what we believe to be error. We pledge to help each other follow the principles of church government explained in The Book of Church Order (BCO) and Rules of Assembly Operations (RAO), as these are the guidelines the Assembly has given to promote purity and peace. We pledge to seek and grant forgiveness, working together to pursue a path that promotes the mutual good. When disagreements exist, we will submit the situation to the group for input and guidance. If there is still no resolution, we will seek the guidance of the Cooperative Ministries Committee (CMC) and submit to their direction (RAO 7-3h). We pledge to cooperate in shared ministry and cooperative projects. Rather than competing through duplicate ministries, we will seek ways to leverage abilities and opportunities for the good of the whole denomination. We pledge to respect the spheres of ministry responsibility God has given to each Committee and Agency through the General Assembly. When circumstances lead to an overlap of spheres (perceived or real), we will seek to pursue mutual benefit rather than individual ministry expansion and control. We pledge to protect the reputation of each other and the ministries we represent. This protection involves believing the best and being slow to believe negative reports about each other (1 Corinthians 13:7). Protection also involves confronting false information and encouraging critics to raise issues directly with the leader of a ministry. We pledge to give and receive constructive criticism regarding our ministries with kindness and patience. Our desire is to help each other serve the Church well by responding to the needs and desires of the members.

The unity we seek, the unity that will lead the world to believe God sent Jesus (John 17:21), is a unity created and sustained by the Holy Spirit. To that end, we seek his blessing:

“May the God of endurance and encouragement grant [us] to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus, that together [we] may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans 15:5-6 ESV).

379

<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=382 printed_page=380 -->

Membership TE Brian Janssen RE Dennis W. Baker TE E. Bruce O'Neil, Chairman RE James C. Richardson, Secretary TE Marvin Padgett, Alternate RE Paul Richardson TE Kevin Rogers RE James D. IRC Officers for 2019-2020 Assembly Year The committee elected as officers: TE Bruce O’Neil – chairman TE Marvin Padgett – vice-chairman (contingent upon re-election) RE James C. Richardson – secretary

The Role of the Interchurch Relations Committee The Interchurch Relations Committee is a Special Committee, functioning under the Rules of Assembly Operations 8-1, through which the Presbyterian Church in America relates to other branches and entities of the Church Universal. The IRC is funded by the Administrative Committee of the General Assembly. The committee is composed of six principal members and two alternates, elected by the General Assembly. The Stated Clerk is a member of the IRC by virtue of his office (RAO 3-2.j). He is expected to communicate with other Reformed denominations (RAO 3-5.e), have an appreciation of the whole Church of the Lord Jesus Christ, and to be able to work with the leaders of all branches of the Church (RAO 3-5.h).

380

<a id="ga47-p383"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=383 printed_page=381 -->

### APPENDIXN

The committee also is advised by TE Cartee Bales of MTW, since some of the work of the IRC relates to churches and Christians abroad, and TE by Billy Park on relations with Korean churches.

Through the IRC, the PCA relates to other Reformed and Presbyterian denominations in North America by participation in the North American Presbyterian and Reformed Council (NAPARC), which meets annually. Through the IRC the PCA relates to Presbyterian and Reformed denominations abroad based in such countries as the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, South Korea, South Africa, Brazil, and Mexico.

The PCA is a member of the World Reformed Fellowship, a fellowship of evangelical Reformed Churches, congregations, institutions, ministries, and individuals, across the spectrum of the evangelical Reformed faith. So the WRF includes Anglicans and Reformed Baptists at the ends of the spectrum, as well as Presbyterians, churches with continental Reformed roots, and Congregationalists in the middle of the continuum. WRF has a General Assembly every four years. The PCA has been a member of the National Association of Evangelicals since 1986. The NAE is composed of evangelical denominations, congregations, institutions, ministries, and individuals in the USA. The PCA Stated Clerk has served as Chairman of the Board since 2006. With the approval and encouragement of the IRC, the Stated Clerk has had contacts since 2009 with evangelical, conservative, orthodox, and traditional renewal groups and newly formed denominations through what is now named the Common Ground Christian Network, formally organized in 2014. “The Common Ground Christian Network is a group of denominations, organizations, congregations, and individuals who believe 21st century Christians need to stand together for the cause of Christ. The common ground upon which we stand is the affirmation of classical orthodox Christianity." Member denominations include the Evangelical Presbyterian Church, the Anglican Church in North America, the North American Lutheran Church, the Evangelical Covenant Order of Presbyterians (ECO), and the Evangelical Association of Reformed and Congregational Churches. The PCA is not a member presently. The PCA and the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod send observers.

381

<a id="ga47-p384"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=384 printed_page=382 -->

The North American Presbyterian and Reformed Council (NAPARC) The PCA delegation to the annual meeting of the North American Presbyterian and Reformed Council consisted of TE Bruce O'Neil, RE James

- **C.** Richardson, TE Marvin Padgett, and TE L. Roy Taylor. The three-day meeting was hosted by the Korean American Presbyterian Church denomination. Fifty-nine attended the meeting, including observers.

The officers for 2019-2020 elected are: The Reverend David Kim, KPCA (Kosin) – Chairman Dr. Anthony Curto, OPC – Vice-chairman The Reverend Ralph Pontier, URCNA – Secretary The Reverend Todd De Rooy, URCNA – Treasurer

The 2019 NAPARC meeting will be in Anaheim, CA, hosted by the KPCA (Kosin) November12-14, 2019. The Presbyterian Church of Mexico, the largest Presbyterian denomination in North America, was invited by the ad interim committee to send observers to the 2019 meeting upon recommendation of the PCA delegation. It was not a unanimous action.

The composition of NAPARC has changed over the years. The Christian Reformed Church of North America was suspended (1998) and then expelled

- **(2002)** from membership for declaring a portion of their constitution "inoperative" by action of one synod rather than going through the proper process of amending their constitution. The presenting issue was the opening of ordained offices to women. The underlying issue was a 1972 Report 44 approved by the General Synod regarding hermeneutics. Since the expulsion of the CRCNA, seven denominations have joined. There are now thirteen member denominations in NAPARC. The PCA comprises 63.5% of the entire membership of NAPARC.

The PCA Assembly in 2006 requested that there be another discussion of organic union. A committee was appointed to come up with a definition of “organic union." Discussion ensued among affinity denominations. Since 1982 there have been no organic unions of NAPARC denominations. It appears unlikely that any of the twelve other NAPARC member denominations will merge with the PCA in the foreseeable future because of the size of the PCA, the ethnic history and constituency of some denominations (ex. Korean, Dutch, French-Canadian), differences in polity (though all are in the Presbyterian polity family), and the desire to maintain certain denominational distinctives.

At present, the second purpose of NAPARC, "to hold out the desirability and need for organic union," is not the primary raison d'être of the council. The first purpose, “to advise, counsel, and cooperate with one another," seems to be taking precedence. The ARPC and RPCNA have had some conversations and simultaneous General Synod meetings, but are not likely to merge. Four denominations of Dutch heritage have been having church union discussions, for example, the CanRC with the URCNA and the FRCNA with the HRC. They have some distinctive theological views, which may be impediments to church union though.

The BPC split off from the OPC one year after the OPC's origin in 1936 over the BPC's dispensational pre-millennialism, total abstinence from tobacco and alcohol, and secondary separation. After the BPC's founder, Carl McIntire's death in 2002, the BPC has had reunion discussions with the OPC in recent years.

Much of the plenary meeting time was taken up with denominational reports of and prayer for the member churches and observer churches.

World Reformed Fellowship The World Reformed Fellowship is a fellowship or network of Reformed denominations (ranging from Anglican, continental Reformed, Presbyterian, Congregationalist, and Baptist), congregations, educational institutions, mission agencies, and individuals. It represents a range of evangelical Reformed thought, polities, ministries, and emphases. On March 31, 2011, the Board of Directors of the World Reformed Fellowship completed work on a Statement of Faith that was five years in the making. Why a new Statement of Faith? There were three guiding motives behind our work: 1) We wished to express accurately the common elements of the historic Reformed Confessions which we have used to define ourselves theologically - The Gallican Confession, The Belgic Confession, The Heidelberg Catechism, The Thirty-Nine Articles, The Second Helvetic Confession, The Canons of Dort, The Westminster Confession of Faith, the London Confession of 1689, and the Savoy Declaration;

2. We wished to bring that historic Reformed orthodoxy to bear on some of the critical issues facing the church of the 21st century abortion, genetic manipulation, the nature of marriage, poverty, suffering, and oppression; and 3) We wish to include the voices of 385

<a id="ga47-p388"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=388 printed_page=386 -->

evangelical Reformed Christians from the entire world, in light of the fact that all of the historic Reformed confessions were written in Western Europe or Great Britain. It has never been and is not now our intention that our Statement of Faith replace any of the historic confessions. However, at the Fourth General Assembly of the WRF in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on March 26, 2015, the members of the WRF determined that the WRF Statement of Faith may stand alongside the historic confessions as one of those to which prospective members may subscribe. Versions of the Statement in the following languages are available as attachments to this article: Afrikaans, French, German, Italian, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, and Ukrainian. The WRF has three commissions; 1) Evangelism and Missions, 2) Theological Education, and 3) Theology. The WRF has regional boards in Africa, Asia, Australia/New Zealand, Europe, Latin America, and North America. The WRF has a General Assembly once every four years. At General Assemblies, we seek to do two primary things: 1) conduct the necessary business of the Assembly (such as considering any changes to our doctrinal standards or our purpose statements and electing the Board of Directors) and 2) addressing major issues facing the global Reformed and evangelical church. The first General Assembly of the WRF was held in Orlando, Florida, in 2000; the second Assembly was held in Johannesburg, South Africa, in 2006; the third Assembly was held in Edinburgh, Scotland, in 2010; and the Fourth General Assembly was held in March of 2015, in Sao Paulo, Brazil. The next General Assembly, The WRF General Assembly 2019, will be held in the city of Jakarta, Indonesia, August 8-12, 2019. The meetings will be held at the facilities of the Reformed Evangelical Church in Indonesia (GRII). Under Article V. E. of the WRF Bylaws the PCA is entitled to five representatives in the bicameral Assembly. Several PCA members will be speakers at the WRF General Assembly; Drs. Ligon Duncan, Richard Pratt, and Peter Jones will be Plenary Speakers. Dr. Kathleen Nielson, of the Gospel Coalition's Women's Ministry, will be a Workshop Leader. The voting representatives to the WRF Assembly will be TE Bruce O'Neil, and RE Paul Richardson, plus three other PCA members who will be attending.

National Association of Evangelicals (NAE) Under the present rules of the NAE, denominational representatives at the NAE are the primary administrative officers of denomination (or their designees in case of absence) depending on the polity of the denomination. So among the Presbyterian-Reformed denominations, the Stated Clerks of the PCA and EPC, the Synod Executive of the Evangelical Covenant Order of Presbyterians, and the General Secretary of the Christian Reformed Church of North America, are members of the Board representing their respective Presbyterian- Reformed denominations. The PCA Stated Clerk has been chairman of the NAE Board since

2006. He chaired a meeting of the Board of Directors of the National Association of Evangelicals October 11, 2018, and March 7, 2019. There is nothing to report to the Assembly regarding the NAE that is contrary to the positions of the PCA. The Stated Clerk provides the IRC members a copy of each edition of the "NAE Update," the electronic newsletter to the IRC summarizing the actions of the NAE. Several online articles and posts inaccurately reported that the NAE at its October 11, 2018 meeting endorsed “Fairness for All Legislation," a.k.a. "the Utah Compromise." The Utah Compromise was a law enacted in Utah that seeks to protect both religious freedom and the basic civil rights of LGBT persons (housing, employment, medical access, etc.) after a Board member shared a portion of uncorrected, unapproved minutes. In fact, no specific legislation was endorsed by the NAE. After the October 11, 2018 meeting, the NAE Office received less than fifteen inquiries regarding the Board's action on the issue of religious liberty and civil rights. That included emails, phone calls, and requests for interviews. A sizeable portion were from a few PCA members, one in particular who made repeated inquiries. Some possible legislation has been discussed among members of the US Congress. On the one hand, The Equality Act would amend the 1964 Civil Rights Act to make sexual orientation and gender identification (SOGI) a protected class but would not offer any protections of religious freedoms. On the other hand, The First Amendment Defense Act would strengthen religious freedoms but does not protect the civil rights LBGT persons already have. Some believe that both religious freedoms and civil rights ought to be protected in a both/and approach rather than an either/or approach.

387

<a id="ga47-p390"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=47 pdf_page=390 printed_page=388 -->

The NAE is on record as affirming that biblical marriage is between one man and one woman and that any sexual relations between people (of opposite sex or the same sex) outside of biblical heterosexual marriage is contrary to biblical teaching. The NAE is on record as affirming religious liberty as guaranteed to every American under the First Amendment of our Constitution. The NAE is on record as affirming that the basic religious and human rights should be protected even though we as evangelicals may disagree with the practices or beliefs of our fellow citizens. The NAE has been, is, and will continue to be committed to biblical marriage and religious liberty. Evangelicals are not of one opinion on the best strategies for protecting our religious liberties under the First Amendment in relation to the civil rights of people whose sexual practices and beliefs we believe to be erroneous and harmful. For example, whether we should be reactive or proactive, or whether the best solutions are influencing public opinion, political activities, legislative action, presidential executive orders, or judicial cases. These are areas where continued discernment is needed. With the increasing secularization of our culture and growing hostility to biblical morality, civil conversation and gracious but persistent advocacy of religious liberties are needed as we seek the best way(s) forward. Overtures have been submitted from Central Carolina Presbytery (2011-12 & 2019-23) seeking for the PCA to withdraw from the NAE. The IRC recommends that Overture 23, "Withdraw from the NAE" be answered in the negative by the Forty-seventh General Assembly. See recommendation 5 below.

Common Ground Christian Network With the approval and encouragement of the IRC, the Stated Clerk began in 2009 to attend the Association for Church Renewal, an association of renewal groups that were devoted to renewal in the mainline denominations. The ACR evolved into the Common Ground Christian Network in 2014, with emerging evangelical denominations from the mainline denominations: the Anglican Church of North America (ACNA), the North American Lutheran Church (NALC), the Evangelical Presbyterian Church, the Evangelical Covenant Order of Presbyterians (ECO), and the Evangelical Association of Reformed and Congregational Churches. The Lutheran Church- Missouri Synod and the PCA send observers. All these groups are stressing the same things, i.e. biblical fidelity, evangelism, discipleship, church planting, and mercy ministries.

5. That the Assembly answer in the negative Overture 23 from Central Carolina Presbytery, "Withdraw from the National Association of Evangelicals." Grounds:

1. Overture 2019-23 repeats many of the same arguments of Overture 2011-12 presented to the Thirty-ninth General Assembly and adds a few new arguments.

2. The Thirty-ninth General Assembly invited Sessions and Presbyteries to comment on the overture before acting on Overture 20011-12 in

2012. Of the 1,455 Sessions and eighty-one Presbyteries at the time, not a single Session or Presbytery submitted a comment.

3. The Fortieth General Assembly answered Overture 2011-12 in the negative.

4. Overture 2019-23 seems to argue that Westminster Confession of Faith 31-4 and Book of Church Order 3-3 prohibit the Church from speaking out on issues dealing with faith and life that are either directly addressed in the Scriptures or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scriptures (WCF-31-6). This is an argument that was advanced in Overture 2011-12. There are differences among us on the present application of the doctrine of "the Spirituality of the Church." Some of our forbearers used that doctrine for the Southern Church not to speak as a body on the issue of chattel slavery on the grounds that it was a political issue. Others of previous generations argued that chattel slavery was a biblical and moral issue on which the Church must speak. The same is true of human trafficking (sexual, economic [slave labor], or child soldiers) and other issues.
